title: Keep Costs Down
description: Optimize token usage. Cache, batching, and model selection strategies.

learningObjectives.text: Calculate cost per agent run using Anthropic's pricing
Implement response caching to eliminate duplicate API calls
Design a model routing strategy (haiku vs. sonnet vs. opus) based on task complexity

contentSections.title: The math that keeps you in business

contentSections.body: Your research agent processes 100 competitor companies every week. Each run uses 50,000 tokens. At Claude Opus 4.6 pricing, that's $7.50 per run — $390/year. Switch to Haiku for the classification steps and cache the research results: now it's $40/year. Same output. 90% savings.

**Token cost basics (Claude pricing as of 2025):**

| Model | Input cost | Output cost |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| claude-haiku-4-5 | $0.80/MTok | $4/MTok |
| claude-sonnet-4-6 | $3/MTok | $15/MTok |
| claude-opus-4-6 | $15/MTok | $75/MTok |

*MTok = 1 million tokens*

**Cost per agent run formula:**
```js
const cost = (
  (inputTokens / 1_000_000) * inputPrice +
  (outputTokens / 1_000_000) * outputPrice
);
// Track via: response.usage.input_tokens + response.usage.output_tokens
```

**Where tokens go in a typical agent:**
- System prompt: 1,000-5,000 (repeated every call)
- Tool definitions: 2,000-4,000 (repeated every call)
- Conversation history: grows each iteration
- Tool results: 500-10,000 per tool call

**Key insight**: the system prompt and tool definitions are paid for on EVERY API call. A 3,000-token system prompt across 20 iterations = 60,000 tokens just for the instructions.

contentSections.question: An agent makes 15 API calls. Each call has a 2,000-token system prompt and 500 tokens of output. Input tokens = 2,500/call × 15 = 37,500. Using Haiku, what's the cost?
contentSections.answer: **About $0.06.** Input: (37,500 / 1,000,000) × $0.80 = $0.030. Output: (7,500 / 1,000,000) × $4 = $0.030. Total: ~$0.06 per run. That's cheap! But scale to 1,000 users running this daily = $60/day = $21,900/year. Cost optimization matters at scale.
contentSections.hint: Use the formula: (tokens / 1,000,000) × price per MTok

contentSections.body: Measure actual token usage before optimizing. Premature cost optimization wastes time. Measure first, cut what matters most.

contentSections.title: The three biggest optimizations

contentSections.body:
**Real-world savings from model routing:**
Before: All 20 agent steps use claude-opus-4-6 → $3.50/run
After: 15 steps use haiku (classification, search parsing), 4 use sonnet (drafting), 1 uses opus (final quality check) → $0.45/run
87% cost reduction. Same output quality.

contentSections.title: Batching and async processing

contentSections.question: Your agent needs to write a nuanced risk assessment that goes straight to a compliance officer. Which model should handle it?

options.label: claude-haiku-4-5 (cheapest)
claude-opus-4-6 (most capable)

feedback.opus: Right — this is a critical_evaluation-shaped task: high stakes, needs the most capable reasoning, worth the cost premium.
feedback.haiku: Model routing means picking the cheapest model that can handle the task — but a compliance-facing risk assessment is exactly the high-stakes case selectModel() routes to Opus, not Haiku.

contentSections.concept: Model routing (the biggest cost lever) means using the cheapest model that can handle each task — Haiku for classification and simple summaries, Sonnet for complex reasoning, Opus only for critical evaluation. Getting this routing right is often bigger savings than any other optimization.

contentSections.body:
**Batching** reduces latency and sometimes costs by processing multiple items together:

```js
// Instead of one API call per item:
for (const item of items) {
  await classify(item); // N calls
}

// Batch them:
const batchPrompt = `Classify each of these items. Return JSON array.

Items:
${items.map((item, i) => `${i+1}. ${item}`).join('\n')}`;
const results = await singleApiCall(batchPrompt); // 1 call
```

**When batching works:**
- Classification / labeling tasks (5-20 items per prompt)
- Independent items with the same output format
- When order doesn't matter

**When batching breaks:**
- Items need different context per item
- Output becomes too large for max_tokens
- Claude's attention degrades on the last items in large batches (real issue)

**Anthropic Batch API** (50% cheaper, async):
For large offline jobs, the Batch API processes up to 100K requests at 50% discount. You submit a batch and get results in < 24 hours. Perfect for nightly processing jobs.

title: Safe & Aligned Agents
description: Prevent hallucinations and harmful output. Keep agents on rails in production.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the three main failure modes of production agents
Implement output validation to catch hallucinations before they reach users
Design a content safety layer for user-facing agent outputs

contentSections.title: What goes wrong in production

contentSections.body: Your agent worked perfectly in testing. Then it went live and told a user that your refund policy offers 60-day returns (it's 30). Or it confidently cited a 'source' that doesn't exist. Or it responded to a frustrated user with 'That's unfortunate, please try again.' Production agents fail in ways tests never predict.

Three failure modes in production agents:

**1. Hallucination** (most common)
Claude generates plausible-sounding but incorrect facts.
- Citing non-existent sources
- Wrong dates, prices, names
- Inventing policy details
*Fix*: Ground outputs in retrieved context (RAG), validate claims against known data

**2. Scope violation** (most dangerous)
Agent takes actions outside its intended scope.
- Answering questions about topics it shouldn't touch
- Performing actions it wasn't authorized for
- Giving advice in regulated domains (medical, legal, financial)
*Fix*: Explicit scope restrictions in system prompt + output validation

**3. Tone/quality failure** (most user-visible)
Outputs that are technically correct but feel wrong.
- Too formal or too casual for the context
- Overly long when brevity was needed
- Dismissive of user frustration
*Fix*: Output format validation + examples of good/bad responses

contentSections.question: An agent generates: 'Our premium plan costs $29/month, which is the industry standard for this feature set.' The actual price is $19/month. What type of failure is this?
contentSections.answer: **Hallucination + scope violation.** The price is hallucinated (wrong number). The 'industry standard' claim is a scope violation — the agent made an unverifiable competitive claim it had no basis to make. Both failures compound: incorrect + overreaching.
contentSections.hint: Is the wrong price a hallucination? Is 'industry standard' a fact the agent can actually know?

contentSections.body: Validate outputs before they reach users. A wrong output that's caught is a bug. A wrong output that reaches a user is an incident.

contentSections.title: Output validation patterns

contentSections.scenario: Your agent is live in production and something feels off about its outputs.
contentSections.question: Which of these are documented production-agent failure modes?

items.label: It generates plausible-sounding but incorrect facts — wrong dates, invented sources, made-up policy details
It takes actions or gives advice outside its intended scope, like medical or legal advice
Its outputs are technically correct but feel wrong — too formal, or dismissive of a frustrated user
It intentionally lies to protect the company's reputation
It crashes instead of responding whenever it's uncertain

explanation.hallucination: Real, and the most common failure mode. Fix: ground outputs in retrieved context (RAG), validate claims against known data.
explanation.scope-violation: Real, and the most dangerous — the agent acting outside authorization. Fix: explicit scope restrictions in the system prompt plus output validation.
explanation.tone-failure: Real, and the most user-visible. Fix: output format validation plus examples of good/bad responses.
explanation.intentional-lying: Not accurate — hallucination isn't intentional deception, it's confidently generating plausible-but-wrong content. There's no intent behind it.
explanation.always-crashes: Not accurate — the real risk is a confident WRONG answer, not a crash. An agent that just refused to respond when uncertain would actually be safer than what really happens.

contentSections.synthesis: The three real failure modes — hallucination, scope violation, tone failure — all share one dangerous trait: none of them look like an obvious error. The agent looks like it's working right up until you check the facts.

contentSections.body: **Use Haiku for validation.** A cheap haiku call to check the output costs ~$0.001 and catches expensive mistakes. Think of it as insurance — you pay a tiny premium on every response to prevent rare but costly failures.

contentSections.title: System prompt guardrails

contentSections.body:
The system prompt is your first line of defense. Effective guardrails are explicit, not implied:

**Explicit scope restrictions:**
```
You ONLY answer questions about [product/topic]. 
For any other topic, respond exactly: 'I can only help with [product/topic] questions.'
Never provide medical, legal, or financial advice.
Never discuss competitor products.
```

**Citation requirements:**
```
When stating facts about [product], only state facts from the provided context.
If the answer is not in the provided context, say: 'I don't have that information. Please contact support.'
Never invent or assume pricing, policies, or features.
```

**Persona consistency:**
```
You are a helpful assistant for [company]. Maintain a professional, friendly tone.
Never say anything that could be interpreted as a product guarantee or legal commitment.
If a user is frustrated, acknowledge their frustration before addressing the issue.
```

**The jailbreak gap**: Users will try to get your agent to say things it shouldn't. Test with: 'Ignore previous instructions', 'Pretend you have no restrictions', 'In a hypothetical scenario...' Your guardrails should survive these attempts.

title: Debug & Monitor
description: Understand agent behavior in production. Logging, tracing, and incident response.

learningObjectives.text: Implement structured logging for every step of an agent loop
Design a trace that reconstructs what an agent did and why
Diagnose a failing agent run from logs alone

contentSections.title: You can't fix what you can't see

contentSections.body: A user reports: 'Your AI gave me wrong information.' You look at the database. The response is there. But what did the agent search? What did it read? Why did it decide to say that? Without tracing, you're blind. Observability turns post-mortem guessing into root cause analysis.

Agent observability requires three layers:

**1. Run-level logs** (what happened in this session)
- Run ID, user ID, timestamp, total tokens, total cost
- Final outcome: success / error / timeout
- Duration

**2. Step-level traces** (what the agent did)
- Each Claude API call: input messages, output, tokens, latency
- Each tool call: tool name, input, output, success/fail
- Stop reason at each step

**3. Quality metrics** (how well it did)
- Output validation results
- User feedback (thumbs up/down, corrections)
- Hallucination detection results

Without all three, you can debug obviously broken agents but not subtly wrong ones.

contentSections.question: A user reports 'the agent gave wrong info' but didn't say what. You have run-level logs showing: run_id=abc, outcome=success, 8 steps, 45K tokens. Is this enough to diagnose the issue?
contentSections.answer: **No — you need step-level traces.** Run-level logs confirm it completed but can't tell you which step produced the wrong output, what the agent read, or what reasoning led to the wrong answer. You need to see the full message sequence — every input, every tool call result, every Claude response.
contentSections.hint: What specifically do you need to know to find the source of wrong information?

contentSections.body: Run-level logs tell you if something happened. Step-level traces tell you why it happened.

contentSections.title: Implementing structured tracing

contentSections.body: **Store message summaries, not full messages.** Full conversation histories can be megabytes. Store the first 200 chars of each response for browsing, but the run ID for reconstructing the full trace from logs if needed. Use structured logging (JSON) so you can filter traces by tool name, error type, cost, etc.

contentSections.title: Alerts and incident response

contentSections.question: Put these incident-response steps in order.
steps: Identify: which run failed, what was the goal
Trace: walk step-by-step to find where it went wrong
Diagnose: tool failure? hallucination? scope violation? context overflow?
Fix: update tool error handling, system prompt, validation, or max iterations
Verify: reproduce the failing case and confirm the fix works
Document: add the failure pattern to known issues, update monitoring
contentSections.explanation: You can't diagnose a cause you haven't traced yet, and you can't verify a fix before you've made one — each step depends on the output of the one before it. Skipping straight to a fix without tracing means guessing at the cause; skipping documentation means the next on-call engineer rediscovers the same failure from scratch.

title: Logging & Tracing Agent Runs
description: Six months from now, someone asks why the agent did what it did on March 3rd. Can you answer?

learningObjectives.text: Explain why standard application logging is insufficient for debugging agent behavior
Design a trace structure that captures each reasoning and tool-call step
Use a trace to reconstruct why an agent made a specific decision

contentSections.title: Why 'it printed some errors' isn't enough

contentSections.body: A customer complains your support agent gave them wrong information three days ago. Your application logs show one line: 'Response sent to user 4471.' That tells you the agent ran. It tells you nothing about why it said what it said.

contentSections.scenario: A customer complains your support agent gave them wrong information three days ago. Your application logs show one line: 'Response sent to user 4471.' That tells you the agent ran. It tells you nothing about why it said what it said.
contentSections.question: What's actually missing here?

options.label: More detailed application logs
A full trace of the reasoning path — every step, tool call, and decision

feedback.trace: Right — a trace records the full reasoning path of one agent run: every think step, every tool call and its result, and the final decision, all linked together so you can replay it.
feedback.logs: Standard logging just records that events happened — a request came in, a response went out. It can't show you why the agent decided what it decided.

contentSections.mechanism: Standard logging records events. A trace records the full reasoning path of one agent run — every 'think' step, every tool call and its result, and the final decision, all linked together so you can replay the run's logic afterward.

contentSections.question: Your trace shows the agent called `search_docs` with a query that was clearly wrong, given the user's actual question. What does this let you diagnose that a simple 'response sent' log entry never could?
contentSections.answer: **Whether the mistake happened in reasoning (a bad decision about what to search) or in the tool itself (a good query that returned bad results).** A single output log can't distinguish 'the agent reasoned poorly' from 'the agent reasoned fine but a downstream tool failed.' The trace's step-by-step record makes that distinction visible, which is the difference between fixing the actual cause and guessing.
contentSections.hint: What could you tell from seeing the query the agent chose to run, that you couldn't tell from just seeing its final answer?

contentSections.body: A trace records the reasoning path, not just the outcome. It's what turns 'the agent was wrong' into 'the agent was wrong because of this specific step.'

contentSections.title: Making traces actually usable

contentSections.body: **Set a retention window and stick to it.** Traces are useful for debugging, not indefinite storage — keep 30-90 days depending on your needs, and delete older ones automatically. Indefinite trace retention quietly turns into a second, unmanaged copy of all your user data.

title: Incident Response When an Agent Misbehaves
description: The agent did something wrong in production. What do you do in the first ten minutes?

learningObjectives.text: Identify the immediate priority actions when an agent malfunction is discovered
Design a kill switch that stops an agent without destroying evidence of what it did
Write a post-incident process that prevents the same failure from recurring

contentSections.title: The first ten minutes

contentSections.body: Someone messages you: 'the support agent just told a customer their refund was approved — it wasn't.' The agent is still running, potentially telling other customers the same thing right now. What you do in the next ten minutes matters more than what you do in the next ten hours.

contentSections.question: Why disable a specific tool ('process_refund') rather than shutting down the entire agent when one capability misbehaves?
contentSections.answer: **Because the entire agent going down is its own kind of harm** — every other function it performs (routing, answering simple questions, drafting) stops working too, for a problem that was isolated to one capability. A targeted kill switch contains the damage to exactly the part that's actually broken, which is both more precise and lets the rest of the system keep serving people correctly.
contentSections.hint: What else does the agent do besides the thing that just went wrong?

contentSections.body: Contain the specific failure, don't reach for the biggest possible shutdown by default. A targeted kill switch, built before you need it, is what makes containment fast instead of panicked.

contentSections.title: After the fire is out

contentSections.scenario: Someone messages you: "the support agent just told a customer their refund was approved — it wasn't." The agent is still running, potentially telling other customers the same thing right now.
contentSections.question: What's the single highest-priority action in the next ten minutes?

options.label: Investigate the full root cause before doing anything else
Stop the specific misbehaving capability first

feedback.stop: Right — stop the bleeding first: disable the specific misbehaving capability, ideally via a per-tool kill switch rather than an all-or-nothing shutdown, since the agent could still be telling other customers the same wrong thing right now.
feedback.investigate: Root-causing matters, but it comes after containment — while you're investigating, the agent could still be actively causing the same harm to more customers.

contentSections.concept: Priority order when something goes wrong: 1) Stop the bleeding — disable the specific misbehaving capability, ideally via a feature flag or per-tool kill switch, not an all-or-nothing shutdown built in a panic. 2) Find the blast radius using traces. 3) Communicate honestly, fast — before affected users discover the problem themselves.

contentSections.body:
Once the immediate harm is contained, the goal shifts from stopping to understanding and preventing.

**A minimal post-incident process:**

1. **Reconstruct the timeline** from traces: when did it start, what triggered it, how many instances happened.
2. **Root cause, not just symptom.** 'The agent said something wrong' is a symptom. 'The tool returned stale cached data that the agent trusted without a freshness check' is a root cause you can actually fix.
3. **Fix the specific cause, and add a check that would have caught it earlier** — a validation, a guardrail, an eval-harness case (from the testing pattern covered earlier) built from this exact failure.
4. **Re-enable gradually**, not all at once — a smaller rollout with close monitoring before returning to full capacity.

The output of every real incident should be a new eval case or guardrail, not just a fix and a hope it doesn't happen again.

**Resist the urge to skip the root-cause step under pressure.** A fast patch that addresses the symptom ('add a disclaimer to refund messages') without the actual cause ('the tool served stale data') leaves the real bug in place, waiting to resurface in a slightly different form.

title: Where a long-running agent actually runs
description: Compute options for an unattended agent — serverless functions, containers, VMs, durable workflow engines — and matching the platform's limits to how long your agent actually runs.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a process designed to run on a laptop fails once it's unattended
Match a hosting option's execution-time limit to an agent's real duration profile
Identify which compute shape fits a bursty task versus a long multi-step one

contentSections.title: The laptop was never the plan

contentSections.body: A team's agent has been running fine as a background process on someone's laptop for three weeks — until the laptop goes to sleep during a run that's halfway through filing a batch of support tickets. Eleven tickets get created, four don't, and nothing recorded which four. Nobody changed the code. The laptop just did what laptops do.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to know what actually broke before they decide where to run it next.
contentSections.question: What's the real mechanism behind this failure?

options.label: The process was never designed to survive an interruption — it held its progress only in memory, with nothing durable checkpointed between steps
The agent's model made an error partway through and stopped itself
The laptop didn't have enough RAM to finish the batch

feedback.durability: Right. Nothing about sleep mode is unusual — it's what laptops do. The actual failure is that the agent's progress lived only in the running process's memory, so anything that stops that process loses everything it hadn't already written somewhere durable.
feedback.model-error: There's no evidence of a model error here — the eleven tickets that did get created were correct. The failure is entirely about the process getting interrupted, not about a wrong decision partway through.
feedback.ram: A laptop sleeping isn't a memory-pressure event — it's an OS-level suspend that any long-running foreground process is vulnerable to, regardless of how much RAM is free.

contentSections.mechanism: 'Unattended' means the process has to survive things a human sitting at a laptop would just notice and restart: sleep, reboots, network drops, someone closing the lid. A hosting choice is really a promise about which of these it absorbs for you and which it doesn't.

contentSections.body:
This is the first real decision in deploying an agent, and it's easy to skip past because a script that works locally *looks* deployment-ready. It isn't, until you've picked something that matches how long and how reliably it needs to run:

- **Serverless functions** (AWS Lambda, Cloud Run jobs, Vercel functions) — fast to ship, scale to zero, but almost all of them enforce a hard execution-time ceiling (Lambda: 15 minutes max; Cloud Run: configurable but capped). Fine for a single tool call or a short synthesis step; wrong for a multi-step agent loop that sometimes runs 40 minutes.
- **Long-running containers** (ECS, Fargate, a plain VM) — no built-in time limit, you own the process lifecycle, which means you also own restart-on-crash, health checks, and graceful shutdown yourself.
- **Durable workflow engines** (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Inngest) — the state of each step is persisted by the platform itself, so a crash mid-run resumes from the last completed step instead of losing everything. This is the closest thing to 'survives anything' but it means writing the agent as discrete, checkpointable steps rather than one continuous loop.

The question to ask isn't 'what's the cheapest option' — it's 'what's the actual distribution of how long a run of mine takes, and does this platform's limit sit comfortably above the long tail of that distribution, not just the median?'
A hosting choice is a promise about what it absorbs for you — sleep, crashes, reboots — so pick it by your agent's real duration profile, not by what's cheapest or fastest to set up.

contentSections.title: Killed at fourteen minutes, no error

contentSections.body: A team moves their agent to AWS Lambda because it's the fastest path to 'deployed.' It works in every test — the test tasks all finish in under five minutes. Three weeks later a real task needs 22 minutes of tool calls, and at the 15-minute mark Lambda simply terminates the function. No exception in the agent's own code, no partial-failure message — from the caller's side, the request just stops.

contentSections.scenario: Before reading on: AWS Lambda has a hard maximum execution time per invocation.
contentSections.question: What is Lambda's maximum execution time, in minutes?
contentSections.explanation: 15 minutes, and it is not configurable upward — it is a hard platform ceiling, the same for every account. Anything that might genuinely need longer than that has to either be split into multiple short invocations that hand off state to each other, or moved to a hosting option without that ceiling.

contentSections.body:
Every compute option has a number like this, and the failure mode when you exceed it is rarely a clean error — it's a silent kill, because the platform assumes anything still running past its limit is stuck, not legitimately working. A short reference:

| Option | Hard time limit | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| AWS Lambda | 15 min | single tool calls, short synthesis |
| Cloud Run (request-based) | up to 60 min, configurable | medium multi-step tasks |
| Fargate / plain container | none | long or unpredictable-duration agents |
| Temporal / Step Functions | none (durable across days) | agents that must survive being killed mid-run |

The fix isn't always 'move to a bigger box.' Sometimes the right fix is decomposing the agent into steps small enough that each one comfortably fits under whatever ceiling you're stuck with — which is a durability property in its own right, independent of which platform you end up on.

A platform's time limit that you exceed doesn't usually raise an error — it silently kills the run, so check the number against your actual duration distribution before you deploy, not after the first real task overruns it.

title: Triggering: scheduled, event-driven, on request
description: The three ways an autonomous agent starts a run — cron, events, and direct requests — and the overlap and idempotency problems each one introduces.

learningObjectives.text: Compare cron, event-driven, and on-request triggering for a given agent task
Identify the overlap and feedback-loop risks each trigger type introduces

contentSections.title: The bot that replied to itself

contentSections.body: A support agent is wired to a Slack webhook: every new message in #support triggers a run. It works well for two days, then someone notices the channel filling with the agent replying to its own replies — a loop nobody wrote, because nobody told the webhook handler to ignore messages the bot itself posted.

contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this webhook handler?

options.label: It never checks whether the message was posted by the agent's own bot user, so its own replies re-trigger itself
It should use a GET request instead of POST
runAgent should be called synchronously before responding to Slack

feedback.self-trigger: Right. Slack's event API delivers every message in the channel, including ones the bot itself sends. With no `event.bot_id` or user-id check, the handler treats the agent's own reply as a fresh trigger, and the loop is self-sustaining.
feedback.verb: Slack's Events API specifically requires POST for event delivery — switching this would break the integration outright, and it has nothing to do with the actual bug.
feedback.sync: Slack expects a fast 200 response and will retry if it doesn't get one quickly — running the agent synchronously before responding is a real anti-pattern, but it's a separate issue from the self-triggering loop.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is a one-line guard: `if (event.bot_id || event.user === BOT_USER_ID) return res.sendStatus(200);` before anything else runs. Any event-driven trigger sourced from a channel the agent itself posts into needs this check, or the agent is a de facto trigger for its own future runs.

contentSections.body:
The three ways to start a run each carry a different failure shape:

- **Scheduled (cron)** — `0 */4 * * *` runs every four hours regardless of whether there's anything to do. Reliable and simple, but wastes runs on quiet periods and, worse, can overlap with itself if one run is still going when the next fires.
- **Event-driven** (webhook, queue message, pub/sub) — reacts immediately to something happening, but has to defend against duplicate delivery (most event systems guarantee *at-least-once*, not *exactly-once*) and, as above, feedback loops where the agent's own output re-triggers it.
- **On request** (a direct API call, someone clicking a button) — the simplest to reason about because a human or another system is deliberately asking for a run right now, but it means the *caller* is now waiting on the agent's full duration, which pushes you straight back into the time-limit problem from the previous lesson.

Picking the wrong one isn't usually catastrophic on day one — it shows up as either wasted spend (cron firing when there's nothing to do), duplicate work (events without dedup), or a timeout in someone's browser tab (on-request without an async pattern).

Every trigger type introduces its own specific failure — cron overlaps with itself, events duplicate or feed back into themselves, on-request pushes the caller into the time-limit problem — so the choice has to defend against the one your trigger actually has.

contentSections.title: Two crons, one job, double the bill

contentSections.body: A daily digest agent is scheduled every 5 minutes as a cheap way to 'check frequently.' Most runs find nothing new and exit fast — but one week the underlying data source gets slow, a run takes 6 minutes, and the next cron tick fires while the first is still going. Now two instances are both writing to the same digest record, and the digest ships twice with different content each time.

contentSections.scenario: The on-call engineer is deciding whether this is a data source problem or a scheduling problem.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism causing the double-write?

options.label: There's no lock or overlap guard, so cron doesn't know or care that a previous invocation is still in flight when it fires the next one
The data source returned corrupted data
Five minutes is too short an interval for any cron job

feedback.no-lock: Right. Cron is a dumb clock — it has no idea whether the last invocation finished, and by default most schedulers will happily fire the next one on top of a still-running one. Nothing in this setup prevents two instances from running concurrently.
feedback.corrupt-data: The slow data source is what widened the window for overlap to happen, but it isn't itself corrupted — the actual bug is that nothing stopped a second run from starting while the first was still in progress.
feedback.interval: Five minutes isn't inherently too short — plenty of jobs run that often safely. The problem is specifically the missing overlap guard, not the interval length by itself.

contentSections.mechanism: A scheduler's only job is to fire at the right time — it is not, by default, a coordinator that tracks whether the last job it started has finished. Any job whose duration can vary needs its own explicit singleton guard (a lock row in a database, a distributed lock, a check-and-set flag) checked at the start of every run, independent of the scheduler.

contentSections.body:
The fix is a lock, not a shorter or longer interval:

```python
def run_digest_job():
    acquired = db.execute(
        "UPDATE job_locks SET locked_at = now() "
        "WHERE job_name = 'daily_digest' AND locked_at IS NULL "
        "RETURNING job_name"
    )
    if not acquired:
        log.info("digest job already running, skipping this tick")
        return
    try:
        do_digest_work()
    finally:
        db.execute(
            "UPDATE job_locks SET locked_at = NULL WHERE job_name = 'daily_digest'"
        )
```

This is a database-row lock, not a distributed-systems novelty — one row, one conditional update, one release in a `finally` so a crash doesn't leave the lock stuck forever (pair it with a stale-lock timeout as a backstop). Any trigger whose duration isn't guaranteed to be shorter than its own interval needs something like this, whether the trigger is cron, a queue consumer, or a webhook that can fire in rapid succession.
A scheduler fires on time — it doesn't know or care if the last run finished, so any job whose duration can vary needs its own explicit lock, not a shorter interval.

title: Secrets and credentials for an autonomous process
description: Scoping, rotating, and never leaking the credentials an unattended agent uses to act on real systems.

learningObjectives.text: Identify why a personal access token reused for an agent is a scoping failure
Design a secret-loading pattern that supports rotation without a redeploy
Evaluate which credential-handling practices actually reduce blast radius

contentSections.title: The token that could do anything

contentSections.body: A developer wires up a coding agent over a weekend and, to move fast, gives it their own personal GitHub token — the one that also has admin rights on the org, access to every private repo, and the ability to delete branches. The agent only ever needs to open pull requests on one repo. Six weeks later, an error handler logs the full request headers to a shared debug channel, token included.

contentSections.question: What's the actual security flaw here, beyond the obviously over-scoped token?

options.label: The error handler logs the full request headers on failure, which for a GitHub client includes the Authorization header carrying the token itself
The function should be synchronous instead of async
It should catch a more specific error type than the generic Error

feedback.logged-secret: Right. `err.request.headers` on most HTTP client errors includes every header sent, and `Authorization: Bearer <token>` is one of them. Logging that object whole means the token — a full org-admin token, in this case — ends up in a shared, probably less-protected debug channel.
feedback.async: Async/await is the correct and normal pattern for an I/O call like this — nothing about sync-vs-async relates to the credential leak.
feedback.error-type: Catching a more specific error type is reasonable error-handling hygiene, but it doesn't touch the actual problem: the token is present in the object being logged, regardless of which catch clause handles it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is two separate things: scope the token down to the one repo the agent actually needs (fine-grained personal access tokens or a GitHub App installation token support this), and never log an error object's full headers/request — log a redacted summary (`{ status: err.status, message: err.message }`) instead. Both matter independently; fixing only one leaves the other failure mode fully intact.

contentSections.body:
A credential handed to an autonomous process should answer three questions before it's ever used:

- **Scope** — what is the *smallest* set of permissions this agent actually needs? A fine-grained GitHub token restricted to one repo with `pull_requests: write` only is a different risk profile from a classic PAT with org-admin, even if both happen to work for the same task today.
- **Identity** — is this the agent's own credential, distinct from any human's? Reusing a person's personal token means every action the agent takes is indistinguishable, in an audit log, from that person acting directly — which makes incident response slower and blame attribution wrong.
- **Lifespan** — does this credential expire on its own, or does it live forever until someone remembers to revoke it? Short-lived tokens (GitHub App installation tokens expire in an hour; cloud STS tokens are similarly short) mean a leak has a built-in expiry, not just a manual one.

None of this shows up as a bug in normal operation — an over-scoped, shared, permanent token works exactly as well as a properly scoped one, until the day something goes wrong and the blast radius turns out to be the whole org instead of one repo.
A credential's scope, identity, and lifespan don't matter for whether the agent works today — they matter for how bad the day is when that credential leaks.

contentSections.title: Rotating at 2am without a redeploy

contentSections.body: An on-call engineer discovers a leaked API key at 2am and needs it dead in the next five minutes. The key is hardcoded into the container image's environment at build time — rotating it means building a new image, pushing it, and redeploying, a fifteen-minute process on a good night. The agent keeps running on the leaked key the entire time.

contentSections.scenario: The team is redesigning how the agent loads its credentials so this never happens again.
contentSections.question: Which of these practices would actually have cut that fifteen minutes down to something closer to five?

items.label: Fetch the credential from a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) at process startup, not bake it into the image
Have the running process watch for a rotation signal and re-fetch the credential without a full restart
Move the agent to a larger compute instance so redeploys are faster
Use a shorter, simpler API key string so it's quicker to type into the rotation form

explanation.secret-manager-runtime: This is the core fix — if the credential is fetched live from a secrets manager at startup (or periodically), rotating the value in the manager is enough. No image rebuild is needed because the image never contained the secret in the first place.
explanation.watch-for-rotation: Going further, a process that periodically re-fetches or listens for a rotation event can pick up the new credential without even a restart — turning a fifteen-minute incident into effectively an instant one.
explanation.bigger-instance: Instance size affects compute speed, not deploy pipeline speed — a bigger box does nothing for how long it takes to build and roll out a new image.
explanation.shorter-key: Key length has no bearing on deploy speed at all — this doesn't touch the actual bottleneck, which is the rebuild-and-redeploy cycle.

contentSections.synthesis: The fifteen minutes wasn't inherent to 'rotating a credential' — it was a side effect of one specific design choice, baking the secret into the image at build time. Fetching it at runtime from a secrets manager turns rotation into a config change instead of a deploy.

contentSections.body:
The pattern that makes rotation fast:

```python
import boto3

def get_credential(secret_name: str) -> str:
    client = boto3.client("secretsmanager")
    response = client.get_secret_value(SecretId=secret_name)
    return response["SecretString"]

# fetched once at process start, or on a periodic refresh timer —
# never hardcoded, never baked into the container image at build time
API_KEY = get_credential("agent/prod/anthropic-key")
```

Rotating the leaked value now means updating it in Secrets Manager and either restarting the process (fast — no build step) or, with a refresh timer, doing nothing at all and waiting for the next fetch cycle. The build-time-versus-runtime distinction is the whole difference between a fifteen-minute incident and a two-minute one, and it costs nothing to set up correctly from the start — it's only expensive to retrofit under pressure.

A credential baked into a build takes a full redeploy to rotate; a credential fetched at runtime from a secrets manager takes a config change — decide which one you have before the night you need to rotate under pressure.

title: Isolation and what it can reach in production
description: Scoping an agent's filesystem, network, and process access to the smallest blast radius it can have and still do its job.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why shared infrastructure between a build agent and production is a blast-radius failure
Design a network and filesystem isolation policy for an agent given its actual required access

contentSections.title: The build server that could reach the database

contentSections.body: A coding agent runs on a shared build server with shell access, so it can run tests and install dependencies. Nobody set up network segmentation between the build server and the production database, because the build server 'isn't production.' When the agent is asked to fix a flaky test and, chasing the failure, runs a diagnostic query against what it thinks is a test database connection string it found in an env file — it's actually the production one.

contentSections.scenario: The postmortem needs to name the actual mechanism, not just 'the agent made a mistake.'
contentSections.question: What's the real cause of this incident?

options.label: The build server had no network boundary separating it from production — the agent's shell access could reach anything the server itself could reach
The agent should have asked for confirmation before running any query
The env file naming was confusing

feedback.no-segmentation: Right. Confirmation prompts and clearer naming are both real mitigations worth having, but neither is the root cause — the root cause is architectural: nothing prevented the build server's network path from reaching a production resource in the first place. An agent with shell access on that server inherits whatever that server can reach.
feedback.no-confirm: A confirmation step would have been a good second layer of defense, but it doesn't explain why the connection was reachable at all — the agent shouldn't have had a network path to production regardless of what it asked or didn't ask.
feedback.naming: Confusing naming made the mistake easier to make, but even with perfect naming, an agent with unrestricted network access from that server could still reach production if it were pointed there — the fix has to be at the access-control layer, not the labeling layer.

contentSections.mechanism: 'Isolation' is really a question about *reachability*: given everything this process can do — its filesystem mounts, its network egress, its shell access — what's the actual set of systems it could touch, intentionally or not? A server that isn't 'meant' to be production-adjacent but has an open network path to it is exactly as reachable as if it were labeled production.

contentSections.body:
Isolation for an agent has three layers, and each one has to be set deliberately — none of them are the default in most setups:

- **Process isolation** — run the agent in its own container or sandboxed process, not directly on a shared host where it inherits every other process's blast radius.
- **Network isolation** — an explicit egress allowlist (only the specific hosts and ports the agent's tools actually call), inside a network segment (VPC, security group) that has no route to production systems the agent doesn't need. Default-deny, not default-allow.
- **Filesystem isolation** — mount only the directories the agent actually needs, and mount them read-only unless a specific step genuinely requires write access. A coding agent that needs to edit files in one repo doesn't need read access to every other repo on the box.

The organizing question across all three is the same: *if this agent went wrong right now — bad output, a prompt injection from something it read, a bug in its own code — what's the worst thing it could reach?* That answer is the actual blast radius, and it should be small and written down, not discovered during an incident.

Isolation isn't about trusting the agent less — it's about making 'what's the worst thing it could reach' a small, deliberate, written-down answer instead of whatever the shared infrastructure happens to allow.

contentSections.title: Writing the blast radius down

contentSections.body: A team redesigning their agent's deployment asks a simple question that turns out to be hard to answer on the spot: 'if this thing were fully compromised right now, what could an attacker actually do with it?' Nobody can answer without going and checking three different config files.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the isolation policy for a coding agent whose actual job is: read one repo, run its test suite, open pull requests against that repo. Nothing else.

options: Read-write on the whole build server
Read-write scoped to a fresh clone of the one target repo, in a container that's destroyed after each run
Read-only on the whole build server
fields.correctValue: Read-write scoped to a fresh clone of the one target repo, in a container that's destroyed after each run

feedback.Read-write on the whole build server: This gives write access to every other repo, config file, and artifact on the server — far more than 'edit files in one repo' requires.
feedback.Read-write scoped to a fresh clone of th: This matches the actual job exactly — it can edit what it needs to, in an ephemeral environment that leaves nothing behind between runs.
feedback.Read-only on the whole build server: It genuinely needs write access to make code changes — read-only would break the one thing it's meant to do.

options: Allowlist: github.com (API + git), the model provider's API endpoint, the package registry — nothing else
fields.correctValue: Allowlist: github.com (API + git), the model provider's API endpoint, the package registry — nothing else

feedback.Unrestricted outbound access: This lets the agent (or anything that compromises it) reach any host on the internet, including internal systems it should never touch — far wider than needed.
feedback.Allowlist: github.com (API + git), the m: This covers everything the actual job requires — opening PRs, calling the model, installing dependencies — and nothing more.
feedback.No network access at all: It needs to reach GitHub and the model API to function at all — zero network access would make the agent unable to do its job.

options: A personal access token with org-admin rights
A fine-grained token scoped to write access on this one repo only
fields.correctValue: A fine-grained token scoped to write access on this one repo only

feedback.A personal access token with org-admin r: This is exactly the over-scoped-token failure from the previous lesson — far more access than opening PRs on one repo requires.
feedback.A fine-grained token scoped to write acc: This matches the job precisely, and limits the damage if the token ever leaks.
feedback.No credential — run unauthenticated: Opening pull requests requires an authenticated identity — this would simply fail.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these three answers individually looks dramatic — a scoped token, an ephemeral container, an allowlist. Together, they turn 'what could an attacker do with this agent' into a short, specific, actually-answerable list: read and modify one repo, open PRs on it, nothing else — instead of 'reach anything the build server can reach.'

contentSections.body: A good isolation policy makes 'what's the worst this agent could do if compromised' a short, specific answer you can state without checking three config files.

title: Rolling out a change to something already running
description: Deploying an update to an agent without breaking runs already in flight — versioning, canaries, and rollback thresholds.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an in-place update to a running agent can corrupt in-flight runs
Design a canary rollout with a concrete, automatic rollback threshold

contentSections.title: The prompt that changed mid-run

contentSections.body: A team ships a change to their agent's tool schema — a renamed parameter, cleaner and more correct — straight to production at 2pm. Runs that started before the deploy are still in flight, holding saved state that references the old parameter name. When those runs resume their next step, they call a tool with an argument name the new code no longer recognizes, and they fail with an error that has nothing obviously to do with the actual change that was made.

contentSections.scenario: The engineer debugging this needs to trace the failure back to its actual cause, not just the error message it produced.
contentSections.question: What's the real mechanism behind these failures?

options.label: In-flight runs were carrying state shaped for the old code, and the deploy replaced the code out from under them mid-execution with no version boundary between old and new
The new parameter name is invalid according to the tool schema spec
The model started hallucinating tool arguments after the deploy

feedback.version-mismatch: Right. Nothing is wrong with the new parameter name in isolation — it's a perfectly valid schema. The failure is that runs already holding old-shaped state got resumed against new-shaped code, and nothing in the deploy process accounted for the runs that were mid-flight when it happened.
feedback.invalid-name: There's nothing wrong with the new schema on its own — it works fine for any run that starts fresh after the deploy. The problem is specific to runs that started before the change and are now colliding with it.
feedback.hallucination: The model isn't inventing anything — it's correctly using the old parameter name it was given in its own saved state. The mismatch is between that saved state and the new code, not a model error.

contentSections.mechanism: A deploy that replaces running code in place has no concept of 'this run started under the old version.' Any run whose state persists across the deploy boundary — which durable, resumable agents are specifically designed to have, per the earlier work on state and durability — needs the deploy to either wait for in-flight runs to finish (draining) or tag runs with the code version they started under, so a resumed run keeps using logic compatible with its own saved state.

contentSections.body:
Two practical patterns handle this:

- **Draining** — stop accepting new runs on the old version, let in-flight runs finish naturally on the old code, then fully cut over. Simple, but means the old version has to stay available (and correct) until the last long-running task finishes, which can be hours for genuinely long agents.
- **Version tagging** — every run records the code/prompt version it started with, and a resumed run is routed back to logic compatible with that version rather than always the latest. More engineering upfront, but it means new deploys never have to wait on old runs to finish, and old and new versions can genuinely coexist.

Neither pattern is 'nice to have' once an agent's runs can span more than a few seconds — an agent short enough to always finish well within a deploy window can get away with neither, but that stops being true the moment a run can plausibly still be going when the next deploy happens, which for most real multi-step agents is most of the time.
A run holding state from before a deploy is a run written for the old version — either drain it to completion on the old code, or tag it so it resumes on logic that actually matches its saved state.

contentSections.title: 5% of traffic, and the number that decides

contentSections.body: A team wants to roll out a rewritten tool-selection prompt without repeating the version-mismatch incident. They send 5% of new runs to the new prompt and watch — and within the first hour, that 5% shows a retry rate more than double the baseline. The rollout dashboard shows the number. Nobody has decided in advance what number would mean 'stop.'

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what specifically makes 'watch the canary and decide if it looks bad' a weaker safety mechanism than it sounds like?
contentSections.answer: Without a threshold set in advance, the decision gets made under time pressure while staring at a live, noisy number — which tends to produce 'let's give it a bit longer to be sure' rather than a clean rollback, especially once some traffic has already gone through the new version.
contentSections.hint: It's not that nobody's watching — it's about when the 'what counts as bad' decision actually gets made.

contentSections.body: A canary only works as a safety net if the rollback threshold was chosen before the rollout started — deciding what counts as 'bad enough' while already watching a live number tends to end in waiting it out instead of rolling back.

title: Choose the deployment shape for seven agents
description: Seven drills applying this module's full toolkit — hosting duration limits, trigger overlap risk, credential scoping, isolation and blast radius, and safe rollouts — to new agent deployment scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply hosting, triggering, credential, isolation, and rollout judgment to new deployment scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against deployment scenarios you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before an agent goes live, check that its hosting matches its real duration, its trigger can't overlap or loop on itself, its credentials are scoped and rotatable, its blast radius is small and written down, and any rollout has a rollback threshold set in advance.

title: Deploy your agent with proper isolation
description: Deploy an agent with least-privilege credentials, an explicit isolation policy, and a documented blast radius — then prove the isolation actually holds.

learningObjectives.text: Deploy an agent with least-privilege credentials and a documented, tested blast radius

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every technique in this module — matching hosting to duration, defending a trigger against overlap, scoping and rotating credentials, isolating network and filesystem access — was building toward one concrete proof: an actually deployed agent whose access is scoped on purpose, with a blast radius you wrote down and then tried to break.

contentSections.title: A deployed agent with least-privilege credentials and a documented blast radius
contentSections.brief: Take an agent you've already built earlier in this track (or a small new one with at least one real tool call) and deploy it somewhere other than your own machine — a container, a scheduled function, or a small VM. It must run on a scoped, non-personal credential; be triggered safely (with an overlap guard if scheduled, or dedup if event-driven); and have an explicit, written isolation policy covering filesystem, network, and credential scope.
contentSections.deliverable: The deployed, running agent; its isolation policy as a short written document (filesystem access, network allowlist, credential scope, and the blast-radius answer — what's the worst it could do if compromised); and a log from at least one deliberate test of that isolation (e.g. confirming it cannot reach a host outside its allowlist, or cannot write outside its scoped directory).

stages.title: Deploy with a scoped credential and safe trigger
stages.instructions: Move the agent off your local machine onto real hosting (container, scheduled function, or VM) that matches its actual duration profile (lesson one). Create a credential scoped specifically to what this agent needs — not a personal token — and load it at runtime rather than baking it into the deployment (lesson three). Wire up its trigger with an explicit overlap guard if scheduled, or a self-trigger/dedup guard if event-driven (lesson two).
stages.checkpoint: The agent is running on real infrastructure, on a scoped non-personal credential, with a trigger that can't overlap with or feed back into itself.

stages.title: Write the isolation policy and blast-radius answer
stages.instructions: Document exactly what the agent's deployment can reach: filesystem (which directories, read-only or read-write), network (the explicit allowlist of hosts it can reach), and credential scope (exactly what the credential can and can't do). Then write one paragraph answering directly: if this deployment were fully compromised right now, what's the worst thing it could actually do? (lesson four)
stages.checkpoint: A written isolation policy covering all three access layers, plus an honest, specific blast-radius statement — not a vague reassurance.

stages.title: Test the isolation and prove it holds
stages.instructions: Pick one concrete claim from your isolation policy and actually test it — e.g. attempt a network call to a host not on the allowlist and confirm it's blocked, or attempt a filesystem write outside the scoped directory and confirm it fails. Log the result. If the test reveals the isolation doesn't actually hold as documented, fix it and re-test.
stages.checkpoint: A logged test that actually exercised one boundary of the isolation policy, with the isolation either confirmed to hold or fixed until it does.

rubric.criterion: The agent is deployed on real infrastructure, not local
rubric.meets: It runs on a container, scheduled function, or VM other than the author's own machine, matched to its real duration profile.

rubric.criterion: The credential is scoped and non-personal
rubric.meets: A credential created specifically for this agent, scoped to only what it needs, loaded at runtime — not a reused personal token or one baked into the deployment artifact.

rubric.criterion: The trigger defends against overlap or self-triggering
rubric.meets: A scheduled trigger has an explicit lock/guard against overlapping runs, or an event-driven trigger has an explicit guard against reacting to its own output.

rubric.criterion: The isolation policy is specific, not generic
rubric.meets: Filesystem, network, and credential scope are each stated concretely (actual paths, actual allowlisted hosts, actual permission scope), not described in general terms.

rubric.criterion: The blast-radius answer is honest
rubric.meets: The written statement names specifically what a compromise could reach, rather than asserting the risk is low without naming what it actually is.

rubric.criterion: The isolation was actually tested, not just documented
rubric.meets: At least one boundary from the policy was tested against the real deployment and the result — pass or a fix-then-pass — is logged.

contentSections.body: An isolation policy only earns trust once something in it was actually tried and shown to hold — this lab exists to replace 'it should be scoped correctly' with a boundary you actually pushed on.

questions.prompt: A hosting platform silently kills a run at its execution-time limit instead of raising an error. What should that change about how you pick where an agent runs?

options.label: Match the platform's hard time limit against your agent's real duration distribution, including its long tail, before deploying
Nothing — every platform eventually raises a clear error when a task runs long
Always choose the platform with no time limit, regardless of the task

questions.explanation: Lesson one — a silent kill at the limit is exactly why the limit has to be checked against real duration data up front, not discovered when a real task overruns it.

questions.prompt: A cron-triggered job occasionally runs long enough to overlap with its own next scheduled tick. What actually prevents the resulting double-write?

options.label: An explicit lock or singleton guard checked at the start of every run, independent of the scheduler
Shortening the cron interval so runs happen less often
Lengthening the cron interval so runs happen less often

questions.explanation: Lesson two — cron doesn't know or care whether the last run finished; only an explicit lock the job checks itself prevents overlap, regardless of interval.

questions.prompt: Why does reusing a developer's personal access token for an autonomous agent create a specific, avoidable risk beyond just 'it's more access than needed'?

options.label: It makes the agent's actions indistinguishable from that person's own actions in an audit log, and ties the credential's lifespan to a human's rather than the agent's actual need
Personal tokens expire faster than service tokens
It's slower to authenticate with a personal token

questions.explanation: Lesson three — scope, identity, and lifespan are the three questions a credential should answer, and a reused personal token typically fails identity (audit attribution) and lifespan (tied to a human, not the task) even when scope happens to be adequate.

questions.prompt: A canary rollout starts showing a worse metric than baseline. What determines whether that triggers a rollback?

options.label: A threshold chosen and written down before the rollout started, checked against a large enough sample
Whether the on-call engineer's gut feeling says it's bad enough
Waiting until 100% of traffic has moved over before evaluating anything

questions.explanation: Lesson five — a threshold decided in advance, applied to a sufficient sample size, is what turns a canary into an actual safety mechanism rather than a slower way to notice a problem.

questions.from: Two modules back — Capstone (An Agent Worth Trusting)
questions.prompt: The capstone module argued that deployment controls (cost cap, kill switch, monitoring) should exist before the first real run rather than being added reactively. What was the reasoning?

options.label: Reactive controls only protect against the second incident, not the first — by the time you add them, the damage from the first one is already done
Regulations require controls to be documented before launch in most jurisdictions
It's cheaper in engineering hours to build all controls at once rather than incrementally

questions.explanation: From the capstone's deployment lesson — a plan to 'monitor and add limits if needed' is a plan that protects the second incident, not the one that actually happens first.

questions.from: Two modules back — Capstone (An Agent Worth Trusting)
questions.prompt: What made the capstone's hard spend cap different from a typical billing alert?

options.label: It was enforced by the harness itself and halted new runs on crossing, rather than just notifying someone after the money was already spent
It used a lower dollar threshold than most billing alerts
It only applied to the model provider's API, not to other costs

questions.explanation: From the capstone's deployment lesson — a billing alert fires after the spend already happened; a harness-enforced cap actually stops new runs from starting once the threshold is crossed.

questions.from: Three modules back — Agents That Talk to People (Support Agents)

options.label: Any autonomous system needs a defined point where control hands back to a human when it's operating outside what it can safely handle — the same principle, whether or not there's a user on the other end
Only agents that talk to users need any human oversight at all
Escalation paths are a user-experience feature, not a safety feature
