questions.from: Four modules back — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: That module emphasized per-item failure isolation so one bad item doesn't sink an entire batch. What's the deployment-layer analogue of that principle for a scheduled or triggered agent?

options.label: One failed or overlapping run shouldn't corrupt or block the state that later runs depend on — hence locks, version tagging, and durable state, not a single shared mutable state that any run can clobber
Batches should always be processed in a single transaction so nothing can partially fail
Deployment has nothing analogous to per-item failure isolation

questions.explanation: Per-item isolation in a batch and run isolation in a deployment are the same idea applied at different granularities: contain a failure so it doesn't corrupt the whole system's shared state.

title: Where the tokens actually go in a run
description: Breaking down a real agent run's token spend by step, and finding the line item nobody was watching.

learningObjectives.text: Break down an agent run's cost by step rather than treating it as one number
Identify which parts of a typical agent loop are the largest, least-visible cost drivers

contentSections.title: The bill that didn't match the mental model

contentSections.body: A team estimates their agent should cost about $0.02 per run, based on the size of the final answer it produces. The actual bill comes in at $0.31 per run — more than 15x their estimate. Nobody changed the model. The final answer really is small. The estimate was just measuring the wrong thing.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to know what their estimate actually missed before they try to fix the cost.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely reason the estimate was off by 15x?

options.label: The estimate was based on the size of the final output, but most of a multi-step agent's cost comes from the input tokens re-sent at every step — the growing conversation history, tool results, and system prompt — not the final answer alone
The model provider silently raised their per-token price
The agent is calling the wrong, more expensive model by mistake

feedback.input-tokens: Right. In a multi-step agent loop, every step re-sends the accumulated context — system prompt, prior turns, every tool result so far — as input tokens, and most providers charge for input tokens on every single call, not just the first one. A run with 8 steps and a growing context can spend the overwhelming majority of its cost on input tokens the user never sees, well before the small final answer is generated.
feedback.price-hike: There's no evidence of a pricing change here, and a 15x miss is far larger than any pricing change would produce — the actual cause is in how the estimate was built, not the price itself.
feedback.wrong-model: This is possible in general, but it doesn't fit the specific pattern described (a fixed misestimate consistent with the output size) — the far more common and structural cause is what the estimate measured in the first place.

contentSections.mechanism: A single model call has one clear cost shape: input tokens in, output tokens out. A multi-step agent loop doesn't — every step re-sends the whole accumulated context as input, so the tenth step in a ten-step run pays for re-reading everything the first nine steps produced. This compounding input cost, not the final visible answer, is where most of an agent's real spend lives.

contentSections.body:
Estimating a single model call's cost from its output size is a reasonable habit that breaks completely for an agentic loop. A concrete breakdown for an 8-step research agent, per step, might look like:

| Step | Input tokens | Output tokens | Running total (input) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (system + question) | 800 | 150 | 800 |
| 2 (+ tool result) | 2,400 | 200 | 2,400 |
| 3 (+ tool result) | 4,100 | 180 | 4,100 |
| ... | ... | ... | ... |
| 8 (final synthesis) | 11,200 | 400 | 11,200 |

By step 8, the input alone is 14x larger than step 1's total call — and every one of those 8 steps was billed on its own growing input. The final answer's 400 output tokens are a rounding error next to the roughly 40,000 cumulative input tokens across the run. This is exactly the shape that makes a per-output-token cost estimate wrong by more than an order of magnitude: the visible, small thing (the answer) is not where the money went.

In a multi-step agent, cost is dominated by input tokens re-sent at every step as context grows — not by the size of the final answer — so any cost estimate has to be built per-step, not from the output alone.

contentSections.title: Naming the four cost lines

contentSections.body: Asked to explain a $0.31 run, an engineer says 'it's the model, it's just expensive.' That's true and also not an answer — 'the model' is four separate things happening at once, and only a breakdown by which of those four is doing the spending tells you what, if anything, to actually change.

contentSections.scenario: Take the 8-step research agent from the previous pod. Roughly what share of its total token spend comes from the system prompt and tool definitions being re-sent at every single step (as opposed to the actual conversation content, tool call outputs, or final answer)?
contentSections.question: What share of total spend, roughly, is the repeatedly-resent system prompt and tool schema?
contentSections.explanation: For a typical setup with a moderate system prompt and several tool definitions, this can easily be 10-20% of total spend — paid eight separate times for content that never changes between steps. It's rarely the single biggest line item (tool results and growing conversation history usually dominate), but it's often the most avoidable one, since a static system prompt and tool schema are exactly the kind of content prompt caching (covered later this module) is built to stop re-billing.

contentSections.body:
A useful mental model splits an agent run's cost into four lines, each with a different fix:

1. **Static context, resent every step** — system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples. Doesn't change between steps, so it's the clearest candidate for caching.
2. **Growing conversation history** — every prior turn, resent as input at every subsequent step. Grows with run length; the target of context-engineering work from earlier in the track and the "cut context" strategies covered later this module.
3. **Tool call results** — search results, file contents, API responses pulled into context. Often the single largest line for research or data-heavy agents, and the first place to look for oversized, unfiltered results being dumped wholesale into context.
4. **Model choice itself** — the same input/output token counts cost dramatically different amounts depending on which model is doing the work, which is the subject of the next lesson.

Naming which of these four dominates a specific run is the actual diagnostic step — 'the model is expensive' collapses four different, differently-fixable problems into one, and picking the wrong fix (say, switching to a cheaper model) does nothing if the real cost driver is an uncached system prompt or an oversized tool result.

'The model is expensive' hides four separate cost lines — static context, growing history, tool results, and model choice — and each one needs its own diagnosis before you know which fix actually applies.

title: Per-run and per-day budgets, enforced
description: The difference between a cost estimate and a cost limit the code itself actually enforces before a run or a day can exceed it.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a monitored cost estimate from an enforced budget
Implement a per-run and per-day spend cap that halts execution rather than just alerting

contentSections.title: The alert that fired after the money was gone

contentSections.body: A billing alert is configured to notify the team if daily spend crosses $100. At 4:47am, a stuck agent enters a retry loop and burns through $380 before the alert email is even opened at 9am — the alert did exactly what it was built to do, and none of it stopped a single dollar from being spent.

contentSections.question: What's the structural flaw in relying on this setup as cost protection?

options.label: The alert is purely observational — nothing in the agent's own code checks spend before or during a run, so crossing the threshold changes nothing about whether the agent keeps running
The threshold of $100 is set too low
Email is too slow a notification channel — it should use SMS instead
Daily spend is the wrong metric — it should track weekly spend

feedback.no-enforcement: Right. A billing alert and a spend limit are different things wearing similar names. The alert observes and notifies; it has no connection at all to whether the agent's own loop keeps calling the model. Nothing about the threshold value, the notification channel, or the time window changes this — the fix has to live inside the agent's own code.
feedback.threshold-low: The threshold value isn't the issue — even a perfectly chosen threshold does nothing to stop spend, because nothing reads it back into the running agent's decision to continue.
feedback.channel: A faster notification (SMS, a page) would shrink the gap between crossing the threshold and a human noticing, but a human noticing faster still isn't the same as the spend actually stopping — it just makes the manual intervention happen sooner.
feedback.wrong-window: The daily window isn't the core problem — a per-run runaway loop can blow through any reasonable daily or weekly threshold before a human ever sees the alert, regardless of which window is used.

contentSections.flawExplanation: An enforced budget has to be checked inside the agent's own execution path, before each model call, with the power to actually stop the loop — not a separate monitoring system that merely observes spend after the fact and hopes someone is awake to act on it.

contentSections.body: A billing alert observes spend after it happens; an enforced budget is a check inside the agent's own loop, run before every call, with the power to actually stop it — only the second one is a real ceiling.

contentSections.title: Per-run versus per-day, and why you need both

contentSections.body: A team sets only a per-run budget of $2 — generous enough that no single legitimate run ever hits it. A misconfigured retry rule causes the agent to be triggered 400 times in one afternoon by a webhook loop, each individual run staying safely under the $2 cap. Total spend for the afternoon: $780.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: why did a $2 per-run cap do nothing to prevent a $780 afternoon?
contentSections.answer: Because a per-run cap only looks at one run's own spend in isolation — it has no memory of how many other runs happened today, so 400 runs that each individually stay under $2 sail straight past it with nothing checking the total.
contentSections.hint: The cap did exactly what it was built to do — every single run really did stay under $2. So what question was it never built to ask?

contentSections.body:
A per-run cap and a per-day cap catch different failure shapes, and neither one alone is sufficient:

- **Per-run budget** catches a single run going wrong — a retry loop inside one execution, an unexpectedly long tool-calling chain, a synthesis step re-processing too much context. It has no idea how many runs happened today.
- **Per-day budget** catches too many runs happening — a triggering bug (the overlap and feedback-loop failures from the deployment module), a spike in legitimate demand nobody sized for, or exactly this scenario: 400 individually-cheap runs adding up to an expensive day.

The two need to be checked together, as the `RunBudget` class above already does — `check_before_call` tests both the run's own running total *and* the shared daily tracker before allowing a call through. A system with only a per-run cap is blind to volume; a system with only a per-day cap can let one pathological run consume the entire day's budget by itself, starving every other legitimate run for the rest of the day.

A per-run cap catches one run going wrong; a per-day cap catches too many runs happening — a system needs both checked together, or it's blind to whichever failure shape the missing one was supposed to catch.

title: Cheaper models for the cheap steps
description: Routing each step of an agent's work to the model whose capability actually matches that step's difficulty, instead of one model for the whole run.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate which steps of a multi-step agent genuinely require a frontier model versus a smaller one
Design a model-routing scheme by step difficulty with a measured quality check

contentSections.title: One model for every step, including the trivial ones

contentSections.body: A document-processing agent uses its most capable (and most expensive) model for every step of its pipeline — including a step that just classifies whether a document is an invoice, a contract, or 'other,' from the first 200 characters. That classification step alone accounts for close to a third of the pipeline's total spend, for a task that doesn't obviously need the same model doing the hard synthesis work later in the pipeline.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to know whether the classification step actually needs the expensive model before they change anything.
contentSections.question: What's the right way to decide whether this step should move to a cheaper model?

options.label: Measure the cheaper model's accuracy on this specific classification task against a held-out test set, and switch only if it holds up within an acceptable margin
Switch immediately — classification is inherently simple, so any model can do it
Keep the expensive model everywhere, since mixing models in one pipeline adds unnecessary complexity

feedback.measure: Right. 'Simple-sounding' and 'actually easy for a cheaper model' aren't the same claim — some classification tasks are genuinely easy for a smaller model, others turn out to hinge on subtle distinctions that only a stronger model reliably catches. The only way to know which this is, is to measure accuracy on your own test set before switching in production.
feedback.assume-simple: Assuming a task is easy because it sounds easy is exactly the mistake this lesson is warning against — some classification tasks that sound trivial (distinguishing similar document types, catching edge cases) genuinely need more capability than expected, and the only way to know is to measure, not assume.
feedback.keep-uniform: Uniformity is a real simplicity benefit, but it's being paid for in real money here — nearly a third of total spend on a step that may not need it. The right response is to check whether the savings justify the added routing complexity, not to rule it out on principle before measuring.

contentSections.mechanism: The instinct to keep one model for the whole pipeline treats model choice as a single decision made once. But a multi-step agent is really a sequence of different tasks — some genuinely need frontier-level reasoning, others are closer to pattern matching that a much smaller, cheaper model handles just as well. Treating them as one decision means either overpaying for the easy steps or underpaying for the hard ones; treating them separately, and measuring each, is what actually matches capability to difficulty.

contentSections.body:
A rough per-step difficulty audit for that document pipeline might look like:

| Step | What it does | Difficulty | Model tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classify document type | 3-way classification from first 200 chars | Low | Small/cheap model |
| Extract structured fields | Pull invoice number, date, amount from varied layouts | Medium | Mid-tier model |
| Flag anomalies | Reason about whether extracted data looks internally inconsistent | High | Frontier model |
| Generate summary | Write a one-paragraph human-readable summary | Low-medium | Small/mid model |

The pattern worth noticing: difficulty doesn't track pipeline position. The last step (summary generation) isn't automatically the hardest just because it's last, and the anomaly-flagging step in the middle can be the genuinely hard one that needs the frontier model's reasoning, while both the step before and after it are comfortably handled by something far cheaper.

Model choice per step should be measured against that step's actual difficulty, not inherited from whatever model the rest of the pipeline uses — difficulty doesn't correlate with position in the pipeline.

contentSections.title: Routing with a measured floor, not a guess

contentSections.body: A team routes their classification step to a cheaper model based on a quick manual spot-check of ten examples, all correctly classified. In production, the cheaper model's accuracy turns out to be 84% on the full distribution of real documents — the ten spot-check examples happened to all be the easy, unambiguous cases.

contentSections.scenario: The team is redesigning how they validate a routing decision so this doesn't happen again.
contentSections.question: Which of these would actually make a routing test trustworthy?

items.label: Pull the test set from real production inputs, including the messy/ambiguous cases, not just clear-cut examples
Use a large enough sample that a handful of unlucky misses don't look like noise or get lost in a tiny total
Just try twenty examples instead of ten, still hand-picked by whoever happens to be testing
Prefer whichever cheap model responds fastest, since speed correlates with reliability

explanation.real-distribution: This is the actual fix — the ten-example failure wasn't about sample size alone, it was that all ten happened to be easy cases. A real test set has to include the ambiguous, harder cases a production system will actually see.
explanation.sample-size: A large enough sample matters too, independent of representativeness — ten examples of any kind, even well-chosen ones, is a small enough number that a couple of lucky or unlucky results can swing the apparent accuracy dramatically.
explanation.more-examples-same-source: More examples helps only if they're actually representative — twenty examples still hand-picked by the same person with the same blind spots doesn't fix the selection bias that caused the original miss.
explanation.faster-model: Response speed has no bearing on classification accuracy — this doesn't address the actual problem, which is about correctness on real inputs, not latency.

contentSections.synthesis: The ten-example failure wasn't really a sample-size problem in isolation — it was a representativeness problem. A bigger sample of the same kind of easy, hand-picked cases would still have missed the same 16% failure rate; what actually catches it is pulling from the real, messy distribution of production inputs.

contentSections.body:
Ten hand-picked examples are not a test set — this is the same lesson the track's evaluation phase already covered, applied to a cost decision instead of a quality decision. A defensible routing decision needs the same discipline:

```python
def evaluate_routing_candidate(step_name, cheap_model, test_set, min_accuracy=0.95):
    """test_set: list of (input, expected_output) pulled from real production
    examples for this step, not hand-picked easy cases."""
    correct = 0
    for input_, expected in test_set:
        result = cheap_model.run(input_)
        if result == expected:
            correct += 1
    accuracy = correct / len(test_set)
    if accuracy < min_accuracy:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{step_name}: cheap model scored {accuracy:.1%} on {len(test_set)} "
            f"real cases, below the {min_accuracy:.0%} floor — not safe to route yet"
        )
    return accuracy

# routing table built only from steps that passed their floor
MODEL_ROUTING = {
    'classify_document': 'small-model',   # passed at 97% on 200 real cases
    'extract_fields': 'mid-model',        # passed at 96% on 150 real cases
    'flag_anomalies': 'frontier-model',   # cheap model failed at 71%, stayed on frontier
    'generate_summary': 'small-model',    # passed at 98% on 200 real cases
}
```

The `min_accuracy` floor and the size of the test set both matter — a floor set too low defeats the point of measuring at all, and a test set of ten cherry-picked examples tells you almost nothing about the full distribution of real inputs the step will actually see. The anomaly-flagging step failing its floor and staying on the frontier model is the routing table working correctly, not a failure of the exercise.

A routing decision built on ten hand-picked examples measures nothing about the real distribution — route a step to a cheaper model only after it clears an accuracy floor on a real, sizeable test set, and keep the ones that don't clear it on the stronger model.

title: Caching what doesn't change
description: Using prompt caching and result caching to stop re-paying for content and computation that's identical across steps or runs.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which parts of an agent's context are stable enough to benefit from prompt caching
Distinguish prompt caching from result caching and when each applies

contentSections.title: Paying for the same system prompt eight times

contentSections.body: An agent's system prompt and tool definitions total roughly 1,800 tokens — modest on its own. Across an 8-step run, that identical, byte-for-byte-unchanged block gets sent as input and billed in full at every single step, because nothing in the setup told the API this content was the same as last time.

contentSections.scenario: Before reading on: an 1,800-token static block gets resent, unchanged, at every step of an 8-step run, with nothing marking it as reusable.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many total tokens of that static block get billed across the whole 8-step run?
contentSections.explanation: 1,800 tokens times 8 steps is 14,400 tokens billed for content that is, byte for byte, exactly the same thing sent eight separate times. Nothing about the content itself changed between steps — the only thing that changed was that nobody told the API it didn't need to re-process and re-bill it in full each time.

contentSections.body:
Most model providers support prompt caching: mark a prefix of the input (the part that doesn't change between calls — system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples) as cacheable, and subsequent calls that share that exact prefix are billed at a steep discount for the cached portion, often 90% or more off, instead of full price every time.

```python
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-...",
    system=[
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": SYSTEM_PROMPT,  # ~1,800 tokens, identical every call this run
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
        }
    ],
    tools=TOOL_DEFINITIONS,  # also identical every call — cache this too
    messages=conversation_so_far,  # this part genuinely changes every step
)
```

The key requirement is that the cached prefix has to be *identical*, token for token, across calls — reordering tool definitions, changing a single word in the system prompt, or inserting something before the cached block invalidates the cache and you're back to paying full price. This makes prompt caching most valuable for exactly the content that's genuinely static within a run: the parts that don't change are the parts worth marking, and the parts that do change (the growing conversation) have to stay outside the cached prefix.

Prompt caching only pays off for content that's byte-for-byte identical across calls — mark the genuinely static prefix (system prompt, tool definitions), and keep anything that actually changes outside it.

contentSections.title: The same question, asked twice, computed twice

contentSections.body: A support agent gets asked 'what's your refund policy' by forty different customers over a week. Each time, it runs the same retrieval-and-synthesis pipeline from scratch — searching, reading, and composing an answer — even though the underlying policy document, and therefore the correct answer, hasn't changed once in that time.

contentSections.question: What's missing here that's costing real, avoidable money on repeated questions?

options.label: There's no result cache keyed on the question (or its semantic equivalent), so an identical question re-runs the full retrieve-and-synthesize pipeline every single time
retrieve and synthesize should run in parallel instead of sequentially
The function should accept a batch of questions instead of one at a time

feedback.no-result-cache: Right. This is a different kind of caching from prompt caching — it's result caching: if the same question (or a close semantic match) has already been fully answered, and the underlying source hasn't changed, there's no need to redo the retrieval and synthesis work at all. Nothing here checks for that before doing the full pipeline again.
feedback.parallel: Retrieval genuinely has to finish before synthesis can use its output — they can't run in parallel, since synthesis depends on retrieval's result. This isn't the actual cost problem here.
feedback.batching: Batching could help throughput for a burst of simultaneous questions, but it does nothing about the deeper issue: even one question at a time, an identical repeated question still redoes work whose answer hasn't changed.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is a cache keyed on the question (or a normalized/semantic version of it), with a value that includes both the answer and some notion of freshness (so a stale cached answer to a policy that *did* change gets invalidated, not served forever): `cache.get(normalize(question))` before doing any retrieval, `cache.set(...)` after synthesizing, with a TTL or explicit invalidation tied to when the source document actually changes.

contentSections.body:
Prompt caching and result caching solve different problems and are easy to conflate:

- **Prompt caching** avoids re-billing for identical *input context* within and across calls to the model — the system prompt, tool schema. It saves on the cost of each call.
- **Result caching** avoids re-doing the *whole pipeline* — retrieval, tool calls, synthesis — when the output would be identical to something already computed. It saves entire calls, not just the input cost of one.

A well-optimized agent typically uses both: prompt caching for the static context on every call it does make, and result caching to avoid making the call — and the retrieval and synthesis work around it — at all, for questions whose answer genuinely hasn't changed since it was last computed.

Prompt caching saves on the cost of a call you're making anyway; result caching avoids making the call at all when the answer hasn't changed — a well-optimized agent needs both, for different reasons.

title: The runaway loop and the bill it produces
description: How a small logic gap turns into an unbounded, expensive loop — and the concrete guards that keep it from happening.

learningObjectives.text: Trace how a small stopping-condition gap produces an unbounded, expensive loop
Design layered guards (step cap, cost cap, loop detection) that catch a runaway independently of each other

contentSections.title: The loop that looked like progress

contentSections.body: A coding agent is asked to fix a failing test. It edits the code, reruns the test, sees a different (but still failing) error, edits again, reruns — 340 times overnight, each iteration technically 'making progress' in the sense that the error message kept changing, never actually converging on a fix. By morning it had run up a bill north of $200 without producing a working fix.

contentSections.scenario: The postmortem needs to identify what specifically let this run for 340 iterations instead of stopping at, say, 10.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that let this loop run unbounded?

options.label: The stopping condition was 'the test passes,' with no cap on the number of attempts or any check for whether attempts were actually converging — so a run that never passes never stops
The model is fundamentally unable to fix failing tests
The test suite itself was broken and unfixable

feedback.no-cap: Right. This is a stopping-condition gap of exactly the shape covered earlier in the track when discussing loop control — 'the test passes' is a legitimate goal, but with nothing else bounding the loop, a run that genuinely can't find a fix (whether or not one exists) simply keeps trying forever, or until something external stops it.
feedback.model-incapable: There's no way to know from this incident alone whether the model was capable of fixing the test in principle — the actual, provable failure is structural: nothing bounded how many attempts it was allowed before someone or something intervened.
feedback.broken-test: This might be true, but it's a separate question from why the loop wasn't stopped — even if the test truly is unfixable, a properly bounded agent should have stopped and reported that after some reasonable number of attempts, not run 340 times.

contentSections.mechanism: A stopping condition defined purely by success ('stop when the test passes') has an implicit, dangerous partner: it never says what happens when success doesn't come. Without an explicit cap — on attempts, on time, on spend — that gap is filled by nothing, and 'nothing' means the loop keeps going until an external force (a person, a platform time limit, an empty wallet) stops it.

contentSections.body:
This connects directly back to the loop-control work earlier in the track, applied specifically to cost: a stopping condition needs at least one of these, and ideally several, independent of each other:

- **A hard step cap** — stop after N attempts regardless of whether progress seems to be happening, e.g. `if attempts >= 15: report_stuck_and_stop()`.
- **A cost cap** — the per-run budget from lesson two, which would have killed this run once cumulative spend crossed its threshold, entirely independent of the step count.
- **A convergence check** — is the *distance* to success actually shrinking, or just churning? 340 different error messages that never trend toward zero remaining test failures is a detectable pattern, not just hindsight.

The reason to want more than one of these isn't redundancy for its own sake — each catches a different way the others can fail. A step cap alone doesn't catch a loop where each step is unusually expensive; a cost cap alone doesn't catch a loop that's cheap-per-step but genuinely never converges over thousands of cheap iterations; a convergence check alone can be fooled by a task that looks like it's making incremental progress right up until the step cap or cost cap would have caught it anyway.

A stopping condition defined only by success has no answer for what happens when success doesn't come — a step cap, a cost cap, and a convergence check each catch a different way a loop can run away, and none of them alone is sufficient.

contentSections.title: Catching it while it's still cheap

contentSections.body: A team adds a step cap of 50 to their coding agent after the $200 incident — an improvement, but the loop from the postmortem would still have run 50 times, at real cost, before stopping. They want to catch a genuinely unproductive loop faster than that, without a cap so tight it kills legitimately long, productive runs.

contentSections.scenario: The team is evaluating candidate signals for detecting a genuinely stuck loop early, before it burns through the full step cap.
contentSections.question: Which of these would actually help distinguish a stuck, unproductive loop from a long but genuinely productive one?

items.label: Track whether the exact same error message (or a near-duplicate) has appeared in the last N attempts with no new information
Track whether each attempt's code diff is trending smaller/more targeted, or staying roughly the same size/scope with no convergence
Just measure how much wall-clock time has passed, regardless of what's happening inside each step
Measure the length of the model's textual explanation at each step — longer explanations mean more progress

explanation.repeated-error: A genuinely productive debugging run usually surfaces *new* information at each attempt — a different error, a narrower failure. Seeing the identical error repeat with no new signal is a strong, specific indicator the loop has stopped learning anything new, even if it hasn't literally repeated the exact same action.
explanation.diff-size-trend: A converging fix typically narrows in scope over attempts — later diffs get smaller and more targeted as the actual bug is isolated. A diff that stays broad and unfocused attempt after attempt, with no narrowing trend, is a real signal of churn rather than progress.
explanation.wall-clock: Wall-clock time alone can't distinguish a genuinely hard, slow-but-productive task from a stuck one — some real fixes legitimately take a long time per attempt, so time elapsed by itself carries no information about whether progress is happening.
explanation.output-length: A model's explanation length has no reliable relationship to whether real progress is happening — a stuck loop can produce long, confident-sounding explanations for a fix that doesn't actually work, just as easily as a productive one can.

contentSections.synthesis: The signals that actually work share a property: they measure something about the *trajectory* of the work itself — is the error space narrowing, is the fix converging — rather than a proxy like time elapsed or explanation length that can be flat or misleading regardless of whether real progress is happening. A loop-detection check built on repeated-error and diff-trend can flag a stuck run at attempt 8 or 10, well before a step cap of 50 would have caught it, while still letting a genuinely converging long run continue.

contentSections.body: A step cap is a backstop, not a detector — a real loop-detection check looks at whether the work is actually converging (narrowing errors, shrinking diffs), which can catch a stuck run far earlier and far cheaper than waiting for the cap to trigger.

contentSections.title: Seven drills

The habit worth keeping: before trusting an agent's cost is under control, check that you know where the tokens actually go, that the budget is enforced in code (not just alerted on), that model choice matches per-step difficulty, that static content is cached, and that the loop has a real convergence check, not just a step count.

title: Cut your agent's cost per run in half
description: Measure your agent's real per-step cost, apply model routing and caching, and prove the cost dropped while quality held on your eval set.

learningObjectives.text: Halve an agent's measured cost per run while holding quality constant on a fixed eval set

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every technique in this module — per-step cost breakdown, enforced budgets, model routing by difficulty, caching, and loop detection — was building toward one concrete proof: a real before-and-after cost number on your own agent, with quality measured on the same eval set both times, not just asserted to be fine.

contentSections.title: Before-and-after cost with quality held constant on your eval set
contentSections.brief: Take an agent you've built earlier in the track, with an eval set from the evaluation phase (or assemble a small one of 8-10 representative cases if you don't have one). Measure its current per-run cost broken down by step. Apply at least two of this module's techniques — model routing for at least one low-difficulty step, and either prompt caching or result caching — then re-measure both cost and eval-set quality.
contentSections.deliverable: A per-step cost breakdown for the original agent; the specific changes applied (which steps were routed to a cheaper model, with the accuracy floor they cleared, and what was cached); a before-and-after cost comparison; and eval-set results for both versions showing quality held within an acceptable margin.

stages.title: Break down and measure baseline cost
stages.instructions: Instrument your agent to log input/output tokens per step (lesson one), then run it across your eval set and compute the per-step cost breakdown and total per-run average. Identify which step or steps are the largest cost line.
stages.checkpoint: A per-step cost table for the current agent, with the largest cost driver clearly identified, and a baseline average cost per run.

stages.title: Apply model routing and caching
stages.instructions: Pick at least one step that's a plausible candidate for a cheaper model, and measure the cheaper model's accuracy against a real test set from that step before switching (lesson three) — only route it if it clears an explicit accuracy floor. Separately, apply prompt caching to your static system prompt/tool definitions, and/or result caching if any step's output is genuinely reusable across runs (lesson four).
stages.checkpoint: At least one step routed to a cheaper model with a measured accuracy floor it cleared, plus caching applied to at least one genuinely static piece of content.

stages.title: Re-measure and report honestly
stages.instructions: Re-run the modified agent across the same eval set. Compute the new per-run average cost and compare to baseline. Run the same eval-set quality check used before the changes and compare scores — report the real numbers, including if quality dropped somewhere and what you'd do about it.
stages.checkpoint: A written before-and-after report: cost reduction as a real percentage, and eval-set quality compared honestly, not just asserted as 'still fine.'

rubric.criterion: The baseline cost breakdown is real and per-step
rubric.meets: Actual measured token/cost data per step from real runs, not an estimate — the largest cost driver is correctly identified from the data.

rubric.criterion: Model routing, if used, was measured before being applied
rubric.meets: Any step routed to a cheaper model was checked against a real accuracy floor on real test cases first, not assumed safe.

rubric.criterion: Caching, if used, targets genuinely static or reusable content
rubric.meets: Prompt caching is applied to content that's actually identical across calls, or result caching to output that's genuinely reusable — not applied indiscriminately.

rubric.criterion: The cost reduction is a real, measured number
rubric.meets: The before-and-after cost comparison comes from actual re-measured runs on the same eval set, not an estimate of expected savings.

rubric.criterion: Quality was checked, not assumed
rubric.meets: The same eval-set quality check ran on both versions, and the comparison is reported honestly, including any regression found.

rubric.criterion: At least a meaningful cost reduction is demonstrated
rubric.meets: The measured cost per run dropped by a substantial, reported amount — the lab's title is a target to aim for, not a number that must be hit exactly, but the direction and magnitude should be real and explained.

contentSections.body: A cost optimization only counts once it's a real before-and-after number on real runs, checked against real quality — this lab exists to replace 'this should be cheaper now' with a measured comparison.

questions.prompt: A team estimates cost from the size of an agent's final answer and is off by more than 15x. What did the estimate most likely miss?

options.label: Input tokens re-sent as growing context at every step of a multi-step run, which most providers bill on every call
The model provider's per-token price had silently increased
Output token pricing is always higher than input token pricing

questions.explanation: Lesson one — a multi-step agent's cost is dominated by input tokens re-sent as context grows, not by the size of the small final output.

questions.prompt: Why does a billing alert that emails the team when daily spend crosses a threshold fail to actually cap a runaway agent's cost?

options.label: It's purely observational — nothing in the agent's own execution path checks it before or during a run, so crossing the threshold doesn't change whether the agent keeps going
Email is inherently too slow a channel for any kind of alert
Billing alerts can only be configured for weekly, not daily, spend

questions.explanation: Lesson two — an enforced budget has to be checked inside the agent's own loop with the power to stop it; a billing alert is disconnected from that loop entirely.

questions.prompt: A team wants to route a document-classification step to a cheaper model. What should determine whether that's safe to do?

options.label: The cheaper model's measured accuracy on a real, sizeable test set from that step, checked against an explicit floor
Whether classification sounds like an inherently simple task
Whichever model is cheapest per token, regardless of accuracy

questions.explanation: Lesson three — 'sounds simple' isn't evidence; only a measured accuracy floor on a real test set justifies routing a step to a cheaper model.

questions.prompt: A coding agent runs 340 attempts overnight trying to fix a failing test, never converging, at real cost. What's the actual gap that let this happen?

options.label: The stopping condition was defined only by success ('stop when the test passes') with no cap or convergence check for what happens when success doesn't come
The model is fundamentally incapable of fixing failing tests
The test suite must have been fundamentally broken

questions.explanation: Lesson five — a success-only stopping condition has no answer for the case where success never comes, and without a cap or convergence check, that gap runs unbounded.

questions.prompt: The Deploying module argued that a scheduled job needs an explicit lock, not just a shorter interval, to prevent overlapping runs. Why doesn't shortening the interval fix the underlying problem?

options.label: A scheduler has no idea whether the previous invocation finished — a shorter interval only makes overlap more likely, not less, if run duration is what's actually variable
Shortening the interval actually does fix it, and a lock is unnecessary extra complexity
Cron intervals can't be safely shortened below five minutes

questions.explanation: From Deploying, lesson two — the scheduler's interval has nothing to do with whether the last run finished; only an explicit lock checked by the job itself prevents overlap.

questions.prompt: That module distinguished a credential baked into a deployment artifact from one fetched at runtime from a secrets manager. Why does this distinction matter specifically for incident response speed?

options.label: A runtime-fetched credential can be rotated by updating the secrets manager and restarting or refreshing the process — no rebuild needed — while a baked-in credential requires a full image rebuild and redeploy
Runtime-fetched credentials are inherently more secure regardless of how fast they can be rotated
There's no real difference in rotation speed between the two approaches

questions.explanation: From Deploying, lesson three — the build-time-versus-runtime distinction is specifically about how fast a leaked credential can be rotated under pressure.

questions.from: Three modules back — Capstone (An Agent Worth Trusting)
questions.prompt: The capstone's deployment controls included a hard spend cap 'enforced by the harness itself.' How does that phrase relate to this module's distinction between a billing alert and an enforced budget?

options.label: It's describing exactly the enforced-budget pattern from this module — a check inside the running system's own execution path that halts new runs, not a downstream alert that only notifies after the fact
It's describing a billing alert configured at the account level
'Enforced by the harness' just means the number is documented somewhere accessible

questions.explanation: The capstone's deployment lesson previewed exactly this module's core distinction — enforcement inside the system versus after-the-fact observation.

questions.from: Four modules back — Data and Workflow Agents
questions.prompt: That module covered per-item failure isolation in a batch — one bad item shouldn't sink the whole batch. What's this module's cost-control analogue of that same isolation principle?

options.label: A per-run budget isolates one run's cost from affecting others, and a per-day budget isolates the day's total from being consumed by any single pathological run or item
Cost control has no real analogue to per-item failure isolation
Batches should always share a single combined cost budget with no per-item separation

questions.explanation: The same containment principle — isolate one unit's failure from consuming the whole system's budget — applies to cost exactly as it applied to per-item batch failures.

title: Tracing a run: every step, input and output
description: Instrumenting an agent so every step's input, output, and decision is recorded as a structured, reconstructable trace — not just a scroll of print statements.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why print-statement debugging fails once an agent is unattended and running many concurrent tasks
Design a span-per-step trace structure that records input, output, and decision at each step

contentSections.title: The print statements that scrolled away

contentSections.body: A team's agent misbehaves in production — it took an action nobody expected. Someone goes looking for what happened and finds... nothing usable. The agent logs with `print()` statements that worked fine in local development, but in production those lines are interleaved with a hundred other concurrent runs' output, unlabeled, and rotated out of the log file after 24 hours. The run that mattered happened yesterday.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to understand exactly what about their local-dev logging broke in production, not just that it 'wasn't enough.'
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that made this debugging impossible?

options.label: Unstructured print output has no run identifier, so concurrent runs' log lines interleave with no way to separate one run's steps from another's
The team should have used a more verbose logging library
The agent's model made a decision that simply can't be explained after the fact

feedback.no-run-id: Right. The core failure isn't volume or verbosity — it's structure. A print statement carries no run identifier, so once two runs are executing concurrently, their output interleaves in the log file with nothing distinguishing which line belongs to which run. Even a perfectly verbose log is useless if you can't attribute each line to the specific run you're trying to reconstruct.
feedback.verbosity: More output would make the interleaving problem worse, not better — without a way to attribute each line to a specific run, additional verbose logging just adds more unattributable noise to sift through.
feedback.unexplainable: Every step an agent takes is the result of a specific model call with a specific input and output — that's fully recordable. The problem here isn't that the decision is unknowable in principle, it's that nothing captured it in a reconstructable form.

contentSections.mechanism: 'Debugging in production' is a different problem from 'debugging locally' primarily because of concurrency and retention: many runs happen at once, and by the time someone notices a problem, the run in question may be long finished and its raw output long gone. A trace has to solve both — attribute every recorded event to the specific run it belongs to, and persist it somewhere that survives longer than a rotating log file.

contentSections.body: A trace isn't 'more logging' — it's structured, run-attributed records of what each step saw, produced, and decided, so one run can be filtered out and reconstructed cleanly from among however many others ran at the same time.

contentSections.title: What a span needs that a log line doesn't

contentSections.body: A team adopts the `RunTracer` pattern and is proud of it — every step is recorded. Then a bug report comes in: a tool call returned an error, and the agent's next step handled it strangely. The trace shows the tool was called and shows the agent's next action. It doesn't show why the agent chose that particular next action given the error — the reasoning step that led there was never captured, only the input and the final output of the step after it.

contentSections.question: The trace faithfully records this step's input and output. What's still missing that would matter for debugging?

options.label: The reasoning that connects the input to the output — why 'retry_with_backoff' was chosen over, say, giving up or trying an alternate tool — isn't captured anywhere, only the two endpoints
The timestamp field is missing
The step name should be more concise

feedback.missing-reasoning: Right. Input and output tell you what happened at the boundaries of the step, but not what happened inside it — specifically, whatever intermediate reasoning or model output led from 'rate limited' to 'retry with backoff' rather than any other option. Without that, a strange decision three weeks from now is just as mysterious as it would have been with print statements, just better organized.
feedback.timestamp: The earlier RunTracer example already includes a timestamp field by default — that's not what's missing from this specific step.
feedback.naming: Step naming is a readability concern, not a debugging-capability one — a differently-named step with the same missing reasoning field would be exactly as hard to debug.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is capturing the `decision` field the `RunTracer` class already has room for — not just the final action taken, but the model's own stated reasoning or the specific rule that produced it: `decision="model reasoning: rate limit is likely transient, backoff-and-retry chosen over switching tools since this tool is the only one that can complete the task"`. Recording only a step's boundaries and skipping what happened between them is a common trace-design mistake — it looks complete because every step is 'there,' but the one thing that actually explains a surprising decision is the part left out.

contentSections.body:
A well-designed span records four things, not two:

1. **Input** — exactly what the step received (the prompt, the tool result, any relevant context).
2. **Output** — exactly what the step produced.
3. **Decision/reasoning** — *why* the output followed from the input, when there was a choice involved (which tool, which next step, why this one). This is the field teams most often skip, and the one most needed when debugging something that looks wrong.
4. **Metadata** — timing, cost for that step, any error encountered, the code/prompt version that was running (tying back to the version-tagging work from the deployment module).

The test for whether a trace is actually complete: could someone who wasn't there, reading only the trace, explain why the agent did what it did at every step — not just what it did? If the answer requires guessing at the model's reasoning, the trace is missing its most important field.

Input and output show the boundaries of a step; the decision/reasoning field is what actually explains a surprising choice — a trace that skips it looks complete but leaves the one thing debugging usually needs unanswered.

title: What to log and what never to log
description: Deciding which parts of a trace are safe and useful to keep, and which create a compliance or security liability the moment they're written down.

learningObjectives.text: Identify categories of data that should never appear in a trace or log, even for debugging purposes
Design a redaction pattern that preserves debugging value while removing sensitive content

contentSections.title: The trace that became the leak

contentSections.body: A support agent's trace store faithfully records every step's full input and output, exactly as the previous lesson recommended — including the customer's full message, which in one case contained their credit card number, typed in by mistake while trying to describe a billing issue. That trace store, built for internal debugging, now contains a stored credit card number sitting in plaintext, readable by anyone with debugging access.

contentSections.scenario: The team needs to understand exactly what went wrong with their tracing design, not just 'don't do that.'
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap between 'record every step's input and output' (the previous lesson's advice) and what actually happened here?

options.label: 'Record everything' was applied without any filter for sensitive content — the previous lesson's completeness goal and this lesson's safety goal are in real tension and both have to be satisfied together, not one traded fully for the other
The customer should never have typed their credit card number into a support chat
Trace stores should never record customer messages at all

feedback.no-filter: Right. The previous lesson's push for complete, reasoning-inclusive traces is genuinely correct for debugging — the gap is that 'complete' was implemented as 'unfiltered,' when what's actually needed is complete *except for* a specific, known category of sensitive content, caught before it's written down at all.
feedback.user-error: Users mistyping sensitive information into a chat window is a real and common occurrence, not a rare edge case a system can assume away — a tracing design that only works when users never make this mistake isn't a safe design.
feedback.no-customer-data: Recording customer messages is exactly what makes debugging a support agent possible at all — the fix isn't removing customer content wholesale, it's filtering the narrow category of genuinely sensitive content (payment details, credentials, government IDs) out of what gets stored.

contentSections.mechanism: Completeness and safety aren't actually in conflict once you separate 'what's needed to debug' from 'what's sensitive regardless of debugging value.' A credit card number typed into a support message adds essentially nothing to debugging why the agent responded the way it did — the fix is a redaction pass applied before storage, not a decision between full traces and safe traces.

contentSections.body:
A short, concrete list of what should never land in a trace store unredacted, because the story above is exactly what happens once you skip this:

- **Credentials and API keys** — even a leaked-key example, per this track's own authoring rules, shouldn't be written out in a real-shaped form; the same caution applies to what an agent might capture from a tool response.
- **Payment details** — card numbers, bank account numbers, anything shaped like a financial instrument.
- **Government IDs and equivalents** — social security numbers, passport numbers, national ID numbers.
- **Full authentication tokens** — session tokens, OAuth tokens, even if they're short-lived.
- **Raw health or legal specifics**, where the domain calls for it — the same category of sensitive personal data that would need special handling anywhere else in the system.

A pattern-based redaction pass, applied at write time before anything reaches the trace store, catches the common shapes without needing a human review step on every single trace:

```python
import re

REDACTION_PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"\b\d{13,19}\b"), "[REDACTED_CARD_NUMBER]"),
    (re.compile(r"\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b"), "[REDACTED_SSN]"),
    (re.compile(r"Bearer [A-Za-z0-9\-_\.]+"), "Bearer [REDACTED_TOKEN]"),
]

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    for pattern, replacement in REDACTION_PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(replacement, text)
    return text

# applied before the trace is ever written, not as a later cleanup pass
tracer.record_step(step_name, redact(json.dumps(input_data)), redact(json.dumps(output_data)))
```

Completeness and safety aren't a trade-off once sensitive content is redacted before storage, not decided between at the level of 'record everything' versus 'record nothing' — a pattern-based redaction pass applied at write time catches the common cases without gutting the trace's debugging value.

contentSections.title: Redacted, but still useful

contentSections.body: After adding redaction, a team finds their traces are now safe but nearly useless for one specific bug — a customer's issue was that the agent got their account tier wrong, and the trace shows `input: "[REDACTED]"` for the whole customer message, because an overly broad redaction pattern caught the entire message instead of just the sensitive substring.

contentSections.scenario: The team is redesigning their redaction pass so it stops destroying debugging value along with the sensitive content.
contentSections.question: Which of these would fix the over-redaction problem while still keeping genuinely sensitive content out?

items.label: Use narrow, specific patterns (card-number shape, SSN shape) that redact only the matching substring, not the whole field
Redact known-sensitive structured fields (a payment-details object) at the field level, leaving unrelated fields in the same record intact
When in doubt, redact the entire message rather than risk missing something
Turn off redaction for internal debugging environments only, since only the team can see those traces

explanation.narrow-patterns: This is exactly the fix — a pattern matched to the specific shape of the sensitive data (like the card-number regex from the previous pod) replaces only the matching substring, leaving the rest of the message, including the account-tier complaint, intact and readable.
explanation.structured-fields: For sensitive data that arrives in known structured fields (a payment form's fields, rather than free text), redacting at the field level is even more precise than pattern matching — it removes exactly the sensitive field and nothing else in the same record.
explanation.redact-everything: This is the failure mode from the hook itself — 'when in doubt, redact the whole thing' is what destroyed the debugging value of the account-tier bug's trace. It optimizes for safety at the total expense of the trace's actual purpose.
explanation.disable-redaction: Internal debugging environments are not exempt from the same leak risk — a credential or payment detail sitting unredacted in a 'team-only' trace store is still a real exposure if that access is ever broader, longer-lived, or less careful than assumed.

contentSections.synthesis: Over-broad redaction and no redaction are the same mistake in opposite directions — both trade away one of the two goals entirely instead of satisfying both. Narrow, shape-specific patterns (or field-level redaction for structured data) are what actually let a trace stay both safe and useful at the same time.

contentSections.body: Redacting an entire field to be safe destroys exactly the debugging value tracing exists for — narrow, shape-specific redaction removes the sensitive substring and keeps everything else intact.

title: Finding the run that went wrong among thousands
description: Tagging and indexing traces with the metadata that makes one specific bad run findable among a day's worth of thousands, instead of searching by hand.

learningObjectives.text: Design tagging metadata that makes a specific run findable by outcome, task type, or user
Evaluate a query strategy for isolating a bad run from thousands of good ones

contentSections.title: Somewhere in eleven thousand runs

contentSections.body: A customer reports that the support agent gave them wrong information about a return policy sometime 'yesterday afternoon.' The trace store has 11,400 runs from yesterday. Every one of them has a run_id and a full span history — none of them has anything that lets the team search for 'the run involving this customer, about returns, that gave a wrong answer.'

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to know exactly what's missing from a trace store that otherwise has complete data on every run.
contentSections.question: What's actually preventing this specific run from being findable, given that all the data technically exists?

options.label: The traces have no queryable metadata — no customer ID, task category, or outcome tag attached at the run level — so finding one run means reading through thousands by hand
11,400 runs in one day is simply too much data to ever search through
The trace store's retention policy deleted the run before it could be found

feedback.no-metadata: Right. The data exists — every run has its full span history. What's missing is a way to narrow 11,400 down to a handful without reading each one: nothing tags a run with who it was for, what kind of task it was, or whether it succeeded, which are exactly the dimensions a real search needs.
feedback.too-much-data: 11,400 records is a completely normal, easily searchable volume for a system with the right indexes — the problem isn't the volume, it's that nothing about these particular records is indexed on the fields that would make searching by volume fast.
feedback.retention: There's no indication the run was deleted — the problem as described is finding a run that still exists among many others, not one that's already gone.

contentSections.mechanism: A trace with complete span data but no run-level metadata is like a filing cabinet with every document filed correctly inside folders, but no labels on the folders — technically complete, practically unsearchable at scale. The fix isn't more data, it's tagging each run at write time with the handful of fields someone will actually want to filter or search by later.

contentSections.body:
A useful minimum set of run-level tags, attached once at the start of a run and updated as the run concludes:

```python
tracer = RunTracer()
tracer.set_metadata(
    customer_id="cust_4821",
    task_category="return_policy_question",
    channel="support_chat",
    started_at=time.time(),
)
# ... run proceeds, spans recorded as before ...
tracer.set_outcome(
    status="completed",       # or "failed", "escalated"
    user_flagged_wrong=False, # set later if the customer disputes the answer
)
```

With this in place, the customer's complaint becomes a filter, not a search-by-hand exercise: `WHERE customer_id = 'cust_4821' AND task_category = 'return_policy_question' AND started_at > yesterday_2pm`. Even a handful of well-chosen tags — who it was for, what kind of task, when, and how it ended — turns 11,400 unsearchable records into a handful of candidates in one query. The tags that matter aren't universal; they're specific to what a team will actually need to filter by, which is worth deciding deliberately rather than adding everything conceivable and diluting the ones that matter.

Complete span data with no run-level tags is a filing cabinet with unlabeled folders — a handful of deliberately chosen tags (who, what kind of task, when, how it ended) turns thousands of unsearchable runs into a one-query filter.

contentSections.title: Tagged, but not on the field that mattered

contentSections.body: A team adds tagging — customer ID, task category, timestamp — and it works well, until a new kind of incident shows up: a specific tool integration started intermittently returning stale data, and every affected run looks completely normal by customer, category, and outcome. Nothing tags which external API version or which specific tool integration a run actually used.

contentSections.intro: The team is expanding their tagging scheme to catch this new failure mode without losing what already works. Assemble the additions.

fields.prompt: What should be added to catch tool-integration-specific issues?
options: Nothing — customer and task-category tags already cover this
A tag recording which specific tool integrations and their versions were actually invoked during the run
A tag recording the total run duration only
fields.correctValue: A tag recording which specific tool integrations and their versions were actually invoked during the run

feedback.Nothing — customer and task-category tag: The hook specifically describes this failure being invisible on exactly those tags — a stale-data bug tied to one tool integration doesn't correlate with which customer or task category was involved.
feedback.A tag recording which specific tool inte: This directly targets the new failure mode — once tool/version is a queryable tag, filtering to 'runs that used the affected integration' becomes a one-line query instead of a mystery.
feedback.A tag recording the total run duration o: Duration doesn't correlate with which tool integration served stale data — a fast run and a slow run could both be affected or unaffected regardless of duration.

fields.prompt: Should the existing customer/task-category/outcome tags be kept?
options: No, replace them with only the new tool-version tag
Yes — they solved a real, different problem (the return-policy complaint) and remain useful for that class of issue
fields.correctValue: Yes — they solved a real, different problem (the return-policy complaint) and remain useful for that class of issue

feedback.No, replace them with only the new tool-: This would reintroduce the original unsearchability problem for customer-specific complaints — different tags solve different kinds of investigations, and this incident doesn't make the earlier ones obsolete.
feedback.Yes — they solved a real, different prob: Right — tagging schemes should grow to cover new investigation patterns as they're discovered, not churn between one tag set and another.
feedback.Only keep the outcome tag: Outcome alone wouldn't have solved the original return-policy complaint (which needed customer_id and task_category to narrow down), so dropping those tags loses real capability.

fields.prompt: When should a new tag like this typically get added, in practice?
options: Only during initial system design, before any real incidents have happened
After a real investigation reveals a gap — a specific kind of question the current tags can't answer
On a fixed schedule, regardless of whether any gap has been found
fields.correctValue: After a real investigation reveals a gap — a specific kind of question the current tags can't answer

feedback.Only during initial system design, befor: It's genuinely difficult to predict every future investigation need in advance — trying to tag for every conceivable future question up front usually produces either an incomplete guess or an unmanageable number of low-value tags.
feedback.After a real investigation reveals a gap: This matches what actually happened here — the tool-version gap was discovered because a real incident couldn't be diagnosed with the existing tags, which is the most reliable signal for which tag is actually worth adding.
feedback.On a fixed schedule, regardless of wheth: A schedule-driven approach risks adding tags nobody needs while still missing the ones an actual incident would reveal — the incident itself is a better signal than a calendar.

contentSections.synthesis: A tagging scheme isn't something to get complete on day one — it grows as real investigations reveal specific gaps, the same way the tool-version tag got added only once a real incident showed customer/category/outcome weren't enough to isolate it.

contentSections.body: A tagging scheme isn't static — new tags get added when a real investigation reveals a specific kind of question the current tags can't answer, and old tags stay because they still answer the questions they were built for.

title: Alerts worth having on an autonomous system
description: Choosing alerts an on-call person will actually trust and act on, instead of a wall of noise that trains everyone to ignore it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a proposed alert is actionable or will contribute to alert fatigue
Design a small set of alerts covering the failure modes this module and the cost module have already surfaced

contentSections.title: The channel everyone muted

contentSections.body: A team sets up alerts for their agent — one for every tool error, one for every retry, one for every run over 5 minutes. Within a week, the alerts channel has 400+ notifications a day, almost all of them for normal, self-recovering hiccups. Three weeks later, a genuinely serious failure — the kill-switch-worthy kind — fires an alert that looks exactly like the other 399 that day, and nobody notices for six hours because the whole channel got muted after week one.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to understand exactly why more alerts made them less safe, not more.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism connecting 'more alerts' to 'the real one got missed'?

options.label: Alerting on every error, including ones the system recovers from on its own, trains the on-call person that alerts are usually noise — by the time a genuinely serious one fires, it's indistinguishable from the noise and gets the same (non-)response
The alerting system itself had a bug that delayed delivery
The team needed a bigger on-call rotation

feedback.alert-fatigue: Right. This is alert fatigue, and it's not a discipline problem — muting a channel that fires 400 times a day for mostly self-recovering issues is a completely rational response to how the alerts were designed. The cost isn't that people are bad at their jobs; it's that the alert design made 'ignore this channel' the correct strategy most of the time, which is exactly what made it the strategy the one time it wasn't.
feedback.delivery-bug: There's no evidence of a technical delivery failure here — the alert did fire, and was delivered to a channel that existed. The problem is what happened after delivery: it looked identical to 399 other notifications that didn't matter.
feedback.rotation-size: More people on-call doesn't fix a channel that's been muted — if everyone has learned to ignore it, adding more people to ignore it doesn't change the underlying signal-to-noise problem.

contentSections.mechanism: An alert's value isn't just whether it correctly detects a problem — it's whether the person receiving it can trust that receiving it means something. A system that alerts on every recoverable hiccup makes every individual alert cheap to ignore, and once that pattern is established, it applies uniformly to the alerts that genuinely matter too. Alert design has to optimize for signal, not just detection.

contentSections.body:
A useful filter for whether an alert deserves to exist: **would a human need to do something different right now if they saw this?** Applied to the three-alert setup above:

- 'Tool error' — usually recovered automatically by a retry. No action needed most of the time. **Not alert-worthy** on its own; worth tracking as a metric, not paging someone.
- 'Retry occurred' — same. A retry succeeding is the system working as designed, not a problem.
- 'Run over 5 minutes' — depends entirely on whether 5 minutes is actually unusual for this agent's real duration profile (from the deployment module). If most runs take 3-4 minutes, this might be meaningful; if the tail is normally 8-10 minutes, it's noise.

What's genuinely worth an alert, matched against failure modes this track has already covered: the daily budget cap being crossed (cost module), a kill switch being triggered or reachable-but-unresponsive (safety module, coming next), an error rate crossing a threshold set relative to baseline (the same discipline as the canary rollback threshold from deployment), and a run failing in a way that required human escalation. Each of these describes a state where a human's response would genuinely differ from 'do nothing' — which is the bar an alert has to clear.

An alert is only worth having if a human would genuinely do something different upon seeing it — alerting on things that recover on their own trains people to ignore the channel, which is exactly what makes the alert that does matter get missed.

contentSections.title: Setting the threshold, not just the metric

contentSections.body: Having narrowed down to 'alert when the error rate crosses a threshold,' a team picks 5% because it's a round number that sounds reasonable. Their agent's normal baseline error rate, it turns out, is 4.3% — meaning the alert fires most days from ordinary variation, right back into the alert-fatigue problem they were trying to avoid.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what should have determined the 5% number instead of it just sounding reasonable?
contentSections.answer: The system's own actual measured baseline error rate — a threshold only means something relative to what's normal for this specific system, and 5% happened to sit almost on top of this one's normal 4.3% baseline, which is why it fired constantly.
contentSections.hint: The problem isn't that 5% is a bad number in the abstract — it's that nobody checked it against anything before choosing it.

contentSections.body: A threshold chosen because it sounds like a reasonable round number is a threshold chosen without data — measure the real baseline first, then set the threshold a deliberate distance above it, with a sample size large enough to filter out normal variation.

title: Debugging a run from three weeks ago
description: Retention, versioning, and context-reconstruction practices that make an old run debuggable, not just an old run's raw data technically still on disk.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what a trace needs beyond raw span data to remain debuggable weeks after a code change
Design a retention and versioning policy that supports debugging an old, disputed run

contentSections.title: The trace that outlived its own explanation

contentSections.body: A customer disputes a decision the agent made three weeks ago. The trace for that exact run is still there — spans, inputs, outputs, decision fields, everything the earlier lessons in this module argued for. But the agent's prompt and tool set have been updated twice since then, and reading the old trace against today's mental model of 'how the agent works' produces a completely wrong explanation, because the agent that ran three weeks ago worked differently.

contentSections.scenario: The team has a complete, well-structured trace and still can't correctly explain what happened.
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap here, given that the trace data itself is genuinely complete?

options.label: The trace records what the agent did but not which version of the agent's code/prompt/tools was running at the time, so it's being read against the wrong mental model of how the system behaved then
Three weeks is simply too long to ever debug anything reliably
The trace should have recorded the customer's full conversation history from before this run too

feedback.no-version-context: Right. The trace itself is complete for the run it describes — the missing piece is knowing which version of the system produced it. Reading a three-week-old trace with today's understanding of the prompt and tools is like reading old code without knowing which commit it's from — the individual facts are right, but the context needed to interpret them correctly is gone.
feedback.too-long: Three weeks isn't inherently too long — plenty of systems debug much older incidents successfully, given the right supporting context. The specific problem here is a missing piece of metadata, not an inherent limit on how far back debugging can reach.
feedback.missing-history: Prior conversation history might matter for some investigations, but it's not what's causing the specific problem described — the issue is interpreting the decision this run made using the wrong (current) understanding of how the system worked at the time, not a lack of earlier context.

contentSections.mechanism: A trace is a record of behavior, not a record of the system that produced the behavior. Without a link back to the exact code, prompt, and tool-schema version in effect at the time — the same version-tagging concept from the deployment module's rollout lesson, applied here for debugging instead of safe rollouts — an old trace gets read through the lens of 'how the system works today,' which can be actively misleading once the system has changed.

contentSections.body:
The fix connects two things this track has already built: version tagging (from safe rollouts) and structured tracing (from earlier this module):

```python
tracer.set_metadata(
    customer_id="cust_4821",
    task_category="return_policy_question",
    agent_version="prompt_v14_tools_v3",  # exactly what was deployed at run time
    code_commit="a3f9c21",
)
```

With `agent_version` recorded at the time of the run, debugging an old trace starts with checking out or reviewing that specific version — the actual system prompt and tool definitions in effect then — rather than assuming today's version explains yesterday's (or three-weeks-ago's) behavior. This is a small addition to what the tracing lessons already built, and it's the one field that turns 'we have the data but it doesn't make sense' into 'we have the data and the context needed to correctly read it.'

A trace records behavior, not the system that produced it — without the exact code/prompt/tool version tagged at run time, an old trace gets misread through today's understanding of a system that has since changed.

contentSections.title: How long is long enough to keep it

contentSections.body: A team asks: 'how long should we retain traces?' One answer is 'forever, storage is cheap.' Another is '7 days, to control cost.' Both are guesses dressed up as policies — neither is grounded in how long a real dispute or investigation actually takes to surface.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to set a retention policy grounded in something real, not intuition.
contentSections.question: Which of these should actually inform how long traces are kept?

items.label: How long it typically takes for a customer, auditor, or internal reviewer to actually raise a question about a specific run (a real, measured or estimated window, not a guess)
How sensitive the redacted-but-still-personal content in a trace is, weighed against the debugging value of keeping it longer
Purely the storage cost, treated as the only variable that matters
Whatever round number (30, 90, 365 days) sounds appropriately cautious without checking against either of the above

explanation.dispute-window: This is the actual driver — if disputes or audits typically surface within, say, 45 days, a retention window shorter than that means the exact trace someone eventually needs to review is already gone by the time it's needed.
explanation.sensitivity-tradeoff: Even with redaction, traces of real interactions carry real privacy weight (this module's own earlier lesson on what to log) — retention length is a genuine trade-off between debugging value and how long that residual sensitivity should be kept around, not a decision made on debugging value alone.
explanation.storage-cost-alone: Storage cost is a real input but treating it as the only variable, as the '7 days to control cost' guess does, ignores whether that window actually covers real investigation needs — cheap storage doesn't make an arbitrarily short window correct, and expensive storage doesn't make an arbitrarily long one wrong either.
