explanation.arbitrary-round-number: A round number chosen for how cautious it sounds is exactly the same mistake as the alert threshold chosen because it 'sounds reasonable' in the previous lesson — it isn't actually grounded in either how long real investigations take or how sensitive the retained content is.

contentSections.synthesis: A defensible retention window is set at the intersection of two real measurements — how long it actually takes for something to need investigating, and how much residual sensitivity is worth carrying for that long — not picked from either extreme (forever, or an arbitrarily short cost-driven cutoff) without checking either one.

contentSections.body: A retention window set purely on storage cost or on a round number that 'sounds cautious' isn't grounded in anything real — set it against how long disputes and investigations actually take to surface, weighed against how much residual sensitivity is worth keeping that long.

title: Diagnose eight runs from traces alone
description: Eight drills applying this module's full toolkit — structured span tracing, redaction, tagging for search, alert design, and version-aware debugging — to new incidents and trace excerpts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply tracing, redaction, tagging, alerting, and version-context judgment to new observability scenarios

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against trace excerpts and incidents you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: a trace only earns its keep if it's structured with a real decision field, redacted at the right precision, tagged with what you'll actually search by, backed by alerts worth trusting, and versioned so it can still be read correctly weeks later.

title: Add tracing and diagnose a seeded failure
description: Build a real trace system for an agent and use only the trace — not the live code — to diagnose a failure seeded deliberately into a run.

learningObjectives.text: Build a working trace system and use it alone to diagnose a seeded agent failure

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every technique in this module — structured spans with a decision field, safe redaction, searchable tagging, trustworthy alerts, and version-aware context — was building toward one concrete proof: a trace system good enough that a failure can be correctly diagnosed using only what it recorded, with the live code deliberately not consulted.

contentSections.title: A trace system plus a diagnosis made using only the trace
contentSections.brief: Add structured tracing (span-per-step, with input/output/decision/metadata, plus run-level tags) to an agent you've built earlier in the track. Apply redaction to at least one category of sensitive content. Then deliberately seed a specific bug or bad behavior into a run (a wrong tool choice, a misread input, a stale-cache issue — your choice), run it, and diagnose exactly what went wrong using only the trace output, without looking at the agent's source code while diagnosing.
contentSections.deliverable: Working trace instrumentation (span structure, redaction, run-level tags); at least one seeded failure run with its full trace; and a written diagnosis produced using only the trace, stating exactly what went wrong and at which step, followed by a check against the actual seeded bug confirming (or correcting) the diagnosis.

stages.title: Build the trace system
stages.instructions: Implement span-per-step tracing with input, output, decision/reasoning, and metadata fields (lesson one). Add redaction for at least one sensitive-content category relevant to your agent (lesson two). Add run-level tags that would let you search for a specific run later (lesson three).
stages.checkpoint: A working trace system producing structured, redacted, tagged spans for a real run of your agent.

stages.title: Seed a failure and capture its trace
stages.instructions: Deliberately introduce one specific bug or bad behavior into your agent — pick something that would produce a genuinely puzzling outcome, not an obvious crash. Run the agent through the trace system and capture the full trace of the failed run.
stages.checkpoint: A trace of a run that failed or misbehaved in a specific, deliberately seeded way, captured in full.

stages.title: Diagnose from the trace alone, then verify
stages.instructions: Without looking at the agent's source code, read only the trace and write a diagnosis: what went wrong, at which step, and why. Then check your diagnosis against the actual seeded bug — if your diagnosis was wrong or incomplete, note specifically what the trace was missing that would have made it possible, and add that field.
stages.checkpoint: A written trace-only diagnosis, checked against the real seeded bug, with an honest note on whether the trace alone was sufficient — and what was added if it wasn't.

rubric.criterion: The trace captures decision, not just input/output
rubric.meets: Each span records what was decided and why, not only what came in and what came out — matching lesson one's four-field standard.

rubric.criterion: Redaction is applied and precise
rubric.meets: At least one sensitive-content category is redacted at the right precision — narrow enough to preserve debugging value, per lesson two.

rubric.criterion: Run-level tags make the run findable
rubric.meets: The trace includes tags that would let this specific run be found later without reading every run — matching lesson three.

rubric.criterion: The failure was genuinely seeded, not incidental
rubric.meets: The bug or bad behavior was deliberately introduced with a known-in-advance cause, so the diagnosis can be checked against ground truth.

rubric.criterion: The diagnosis was made from the trace alone
rubric.meets: The diagnosis was written without consulting the agent's source code, using only what the trace recorded.

rubric.criterion: The result is reported honestly
rubric.meets: The diagnosis is checked against the real seeded bug and the report says plainly whether it was correct, and if not, what the trace was missing.

contentSections.body: A trace system only proves itself once a real diagnosis was made from it alone and checked against ground truth — this lab exists to replace 'the trace should have everything we need' with an actual test of whether it does.

title: Checkpoint — Seeing What It Did
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from Cost Control (the previous module in this phase), 2 from Deploying.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's observability vocabulary and how it connects to cost and deployment controls covered previously

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Seeing What It Did
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.from: This module — Seeing What It Did
questions.prompt: Why do print statements fail as a debugging strategy once an agent has multiple concurrent runs in production?

options.label: Print output carries no run identifier, so concurrent runs' lines interleave with no way to attribute a line to the specific run being investigated
Print statements are always too slow to execute in production
Production environments technically disable the print function

questions.explanation: Lesson one — the core failure is structural (no run attribution), not about speed or availability of the print function itself.

questions.from: This module — Seeing What It Did
questions.prompt: A team redacts an entire customer message field whenever any sensitive pattern is detected anywhere in it, and loses the ability to debug an unrelated complaint in that same message. What should the redaction have done instead?

options.label: Matched and replaced only the specific sensitive substring (via a narrow, shape-specific pattern), leaving the rest of the message intact
Redacted the entire trace, not just the message field, to be extra safe
Disabled redaction entirely since it was causing debugging problems

questions.explanation: Lesson two — narrow, shape-specific redaction preserves debugging value while still removing genuinely sensitive content; over-broad redaction and no redaction are the same mistake in opposite directions.

questions.from: This module — Seeing What It Did
questions.prompt: A trace store has complete data on 11,400 runs from yesterday, but finding one specific customer's disputed run means reading through them by hand. What's missing?

options.label: Run-level metadata tags (customer ID, task category, outcome) set at write time, so the run can be found with a filter instead of a manual search
More detailed span data within each individual run
A larger trace storage system, since 11,400 runs is too much data

questions.explanation: Lesson three — the data exists; what's missing is queryable metadata that turns a search-by-hand into a filter, independent of how much span detail each run already has.

questions.from: This module — Seeing What It Did
questions.prompt: A team's alert channel fires 400+ times a day and gets muted, causing a genuinely serious failure to be missed for six hours. What's the actual mechanism connecting the two?

options.label: Alerting on things that recover on their own trains the on-call person that alerts are usually noise, so the one that matters looks indistinguishable from the 399 that didn't and gets the same non-response
The alerting system had a technical delivery failure
The on-call rotation was too small to handle the volume

questions.explanation: Lesson four — alert fatigue is the mechanism; an over-broad alert design makes ignoring the channel the rational response most of the time, which is exactly what causes the real alert to be missed.

questions.prompt: That module distinguished a billing alert from an enforced budget. What made the enforced version actually stop spend where the alert didn't?

options.label: The enforced budget was checked inside the agent's own execution path before each call, with the power to halt the run — the alert only observed and notified after spend already happened
The enforced budget used a lower dollar threshold
The alert and the enforced budget were functionally identical, just named differently

questions.explanation: From Cost Control, lesson two — the enforcement location (inside the loop, before spending) is what actually stops the money, not the threshold value or the naming.

questions.prompt: That module's runaway-loop lesson distinguished a hard step cap from a convergence check. Why does a convergence check catch a stuck loop earlier than a step cap alone?

options.label: A convergence check examines whether the work is actually trending toward success (narrowing errors, shrinking diffs), while a step cap is blind to that and only stops once the count is reached regardless of whether progress was ever happening
A step cap and a convergence check catch a stuck loop at exactly the same point
A convergence check is just a step cap set to a smaller number

questions.explanation: From Cost Control, lesson five — a convergence check looks at trajectory, which lets it flag a stuck loop well before a step cap's fixed count would.

questions.prompt: That module argued a canary rollout needs a rollback threshold set before the rollout starts, not decided while watching a live number. What's the parallel principle this module applied to alert thresholds?

options.label: An alert threshold should be set against a measured baseline in advance, not chosen because it's a round number that sounds reasonable — the same discipline, applied to a different decision
Alert thresholds and rollback thresholds are unrelated concepts with no shared principle
Both should always be set to exactly the same numeric value regardless of context

questions.explanation: This module's alert-threshold lesson explicitly reused the deployment module's canary-threshold discipline — measure the baseline first, then set the threshold a deliberate distance above it.

questions.prompt: That module's rollout lesson introduced version-tagging a run so it resumes on logic compatible with its own saved state. How did this module reuse that same idea for a different purpose?

options.label: Tagging a trace with the exact agent/code version running at the time, so an old trace can be correctly interpreted against the system as it actually was then, not against today's version
This module didn't reuse that idea — tracing and rollout versioning are unrelated
Version tagging is only useful for preventing deploy-time crashes, not for later debugging

questions.explanation: This module's final lesson directly reused version-tagging — originally built to keep in-flight runs safe during a rollout — to keep old traces correctly interpretable weeks after the system has changed.

title: Actions that must never be automatic
description: Identifying which of an agent's possible actions are irreversible or high-stakes enough that they require a human in the loop before execution, not after.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish reversible from irreversible actions in an agent's action space
Evaluate which actions in a given agent's toolkit require human approval before execution

contentSections.title: The refund that couldn't be undone

contentSections.body: A support agent is given a `process_refund` tool so it can resolve billing disputes without waiting on a human. It works well for two weeks, then a confused customer's ambiguous message gets misread as a refund request for the wrong amount — a $4,200 enterprise invoice instead of a $42 line item. The refund tool executes immediately, the money moves, and by the time anyone notices, reversing it means chasing the bank, not undoing a database row.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to name exactly what made this specific mistake so costly, not just 'the agent misread a message.'
contentSections.question: What's the real design flaw, independent of whether the misread itself could have been prevented?

options.label: A tool that produces an irreversible real-world effect (money leaving an account) was wired to execute directly from the agent's own decision, with no human checkpoint between the decision and the action actually happening
The agent's language understanding needs to improve before it can be trusted with any tools
Refund amounts should always be capped at a fixed maximum, regardless of the situation

feedback.no-checkpoint: Right. Misreads and mistakes are going to happen — that's true of any system, human or automated. The actual design flaw is independent of this particular mistake: an irreversible, high-stakes action was allowed to execute the moment the agent decided to take it, with nothing between decision and execution that a human could catch it at.
feedback.understanding: Language understanding will never be perfect, for any system — designing safety around 'wait until misreads never happen' is designing around an assumption that will never hold. The fix has to work even when a misread does happen.
feedback.cap-only: A cap is a reasonable additional control, but it doesn't solve the general problem — even a capped refund amount can still be wrong, sent to the wrong party, or triggered by the wrong misread, and a cap alone still lets the wrong action execute automatically up to that ceiling.

contentSections.mechanism: Not every mistake is equally costly, because not every action is equally reversible. A wrongly-drafted email that hasn't been sent yet costs nothing to fix. A refund that's already left the account, a production database row that's already been deleted, or a message that's already been sent to an external party — these are different in kind, not just degree, because undoing them after the fact ranges from expensive to genuinely impossible. The design question isn't 'how do we make the agent never wrong' — it's 'which of its possible actions can't be taken back, and does a human see those before they happen.'

contentSections.body:
A useful first pass at sorting an agent's action space:

| Action | Reversible? | Automatic OK? |
|---|---|---|
| Draft a reply, save as unsent | Yes — nothing happened yet | Yes |
| Query a database (read-only) | Yes — no state changed | Yes |
| Send an external email | No — recipient has seen it | Requires approval |
| Issue a refund | No — money moved | Requires approval |
| Delete a production record | Often no — depends on backups/soft-delete | Requires approval |
| Post to a public channel | No — visible immediately | Requires approval |

The pattern: reversibility, not perceived risk or dollar amount alone, is the organizing question. A $5 refund and a $5,000 refund are the same *kind* of action — irreversible, external, money-moving — even though one obviously sounds less alarming. Treating them differently by amount alone (as the cap-only answer above tried to do) misses that the mechanism of harm is identical; only the magnitude differs, and a wrong $5 refund to the wrong person is still a mistake that happened without anyone catching it first.

The organizing question for whether an action needs human approval isn't how risky it sounds or how large the number is — it's whether it can be undone after the fact. Irreversible actions need a checkpoint before execution; reversible ones don't.

contentSections.title: Reversible in theory, not in practice

contentSections.body: A team reasons that deleting a database record is 'technically reversible' because backups exist, so they let their data-cleanup agent delete records automatically. The backup restore process, it turns out, takes four hours, requires a senior engineer's approval, and restores the entire table to a point-in-time snapshot — meaning any other legitimate change made to that table in the meantime gets lost too.

contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in using this as the test for whether an action can skip human approval?

options.label: 'A backup exists' and 'reversal is fast, clean, and low-cost enough to actually happen in practice' are different claims — a technically-possible-but-expensive restore functions like an irreversible action for any practical purpose
The function should check for backup existence using a different data type
Backups should be checked more frequently, on a shorter interval

feedback.practical-cost: Right. A four-hour, senior-engineer-gated, all-or-nothing restore is 'reversible' in the narrowest technical sense and functions like an irreversible action for any realistic operational purpose — nobody's going to trigger that process to fix one bad delete, and even if they do, it costs other legitimate changes made in the meantime. The check needs to ask about *practical* reversibility, not just whether a backup exists somewhere.
feedback.type: The data type of the check isn't the issue — even a perfectly-typed boolean check based on 'does a backup exist' still asks the wrong question about what actually counts as reversible in practice.
feedback.backup-frequency: More frequent backups might reduce data loss in a restore, but it doesn't change the fundamental problem: the restore process itself is still slow, gated, and costly to actually invoke, regardless of how fresh the backup is.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A more honest reversibility check asks about the actual cost and speed of undoing the action, not just whether undoing is theoretically possible: `isPracticallyReversible(action)` should weigh restore time, who has to approve it, and whether the restore itself has side effects (like losing other legitimate changes) — and if any of those make reversal expensive or slow enough that nobody would realistically do it for a single mistake, the action should be treated as irreversible for approval purposes, regardless of what a backup log technically allows.

contentSections.body: This distinction — technical reversibility versus practical reversibility — is the same trap as an unenforced budget or an untested isolation boundary from earlier modules: a control that exists on paper but doesn't actually function under real conditions isn't a control. The test worth applying to every action in an agent's toolkit: if this goes wrong, would someone actually, realistically undo it within a timeframe that matters — cheaply, without a multi-hour process, without losing other legitimate work? If the honest answer is no, it belongs in the requires-approval category, whatever a backup policy technically permits.

A backup existing doesn't make an action practically reversible if restoring it is slow, gated, or costly enough that nobody would realistically do it for one mistake — treat an action as irreversible unless undoing it is actually cheap and fast in practice, not just theoretically possible.

title: Approval steps that people actually read
description: Designing an approval request so the human reviewing it can actually catch a mistake, instead of rubber-stamping a wall of text they've learned to skip.

learningObjectives.text: Identify why an approval step can exist and still fail to catch a mistake
Design an approval request that surfaces the specific decision a human needs to make

contentSections.title: Approved without being read

contentSections.body: A team adds a human-approval step before every refund, exactly as the previous lesson recommended — and the $4,200 mistake happens anyway. The approval request that went to the on-call reviewer was a raw JSON dump of the full agent context: 40 lines of tool call history, system state, and conversation log, with the actual refund amount buried in line 31. The reviewer, three requests deep into a busy afternoon, clicks approve without reading past line 3.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to know why having an approval step didn't actually prevent the mistake it was built to catch.
contentSections.question: What's the real mechanism behind the approval step failing here?

options.label: The approval request presented the decision buried in irrelevant detail, so it functioned as a rubber-stamp click rather than something a busy human could actually evaluate in the time they realistically have
The reviewer wasn't paying enough attention and needs more training
Approval steps don't actually prevent mistakes and shouldn't be relied on

feedback.buried-decision: Right. A person reviewing their fifth approval request of the afternoon, faced with 40 lines of raw context, is not going to reliably find the one number that matters on line 31 — this isn't a discipline failure, it's what happens when a UI design makes the actual decision hard to find. The gate existed structurally, but nothing about its presentation made the decision reviewable in practice.
feedback.reviewer-fault: Blaming the reviewer treats this as an individual failing rather than a systemic one — the exact same reviewer, shown a request that surfaces 'refund $4,200 to acct #8821, is this expected?' in the first line, would very likely have caught it. The design, not the person, is what changed the outcome.
feedback.approval-useless: The previous pod's lesson wasn't that approval steps are pointless — it's that this specific one was designed in a way that defeated its own purpose. A well-designed approval step (the subject of the rest of this lesson) genuinely does catch mistakes; this one just wasn't built that way.

contentSections.mechanism: An approval gate's real function is to put a specific, reviewable decision in front of a human at the moment it matters. A raw context dump technically satisfies 'a human has to click something' while completely failing that actual function — it optimizes for the checkbox existing, not for the decision being something a time-pressured person can actually evaluate.

contentSections.body:
A well-designed approval request answers three questions in the first few seconds someone looks at it, not buried on line 31:

```json
{
  "action": "process_refund",
  "summary": "Refund $4,200.00 to account #8821 (Acme Corp) for invoice #INV-2291",
  "why_flagged": "Amount exceeds the $500 auto-approval threshold",
  "context": "Customer message: 'can you look into the charge on invoice 2291, something seems off' — the agent interpreted this as a full-amount refund request",
  "agent_confidence": "medium — the customer's message did not explicitly request a refund of this specific amount"
}
```

The design goal is that a reviewer can answer 'does this look right' from the summary and why-flagged fields alone, in the time they'd actually spend on it — and can drill into the raw context only if something in that summary looks off, rather than being required to parse the full context every time just to find the one relevant fact. Note the `agent_confidence` field here specifically: it flags that the customer's message was ambiguous, exactly the kind of signal that would have caught this mistake if it had been surfaced instead of buried.

An approval request that requires parsing 40 lines to find the decision functions as a rubber stamp, whatever it was designed to do — a good one puts the specific decision, and why it was flagged, in the first few lines.

contentSections.title: The threshold that got approved every single time

contentSections.body: After redesigning the approval request format, a team notices something else: 94% of refund approvals over the last month were approved with no changes, in under 10 seconds each. They're not sure if this means the agent is doing a great job, or the reviewers have started treating approval as a formality again — the two look identical from the approval logs alone.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to distinguish 'the agent is genuinely reliable, so fast approvals are appropriate' from 'reviewers have gone back to rubber-stamping' using data they can actually collect.
contentSections.question: Which of these would help tell the two apart?

items.label: Periodically seed a deliberately wrong request into the approval queue (with reviewer awareness this happens) and check whether it gets caught
Look at whether approval times cluster suspiciously tightly (everyone taking almost exactly the same few seconds) versus varying with request complexity
Just look at the overall approval rate — a high rate on its own tells you which explanation is true
Ask reviewers in a survey whether they feel like they're paying enough attention

explanation.seed-test-cases: A deliberately seeded bad request, with reviewers aware this practice exists (an important ethical detail — this shouldn't be a secret trap), directly tests whether the approval step is functioning: if seeded bad requests get caught reliably, that's real evidence reviewers are actually evaluating requests, not just clicking through.
explanation.time-distribution: Genuine review takes variable time depending on how much scrutiny a specific request needs — near-uniform, very fast approval times across genuinely different requests is a real behavioral signal of rubber-stamping, independent of what anyone reports about their own attention.
explanation.approval-rate-alone: A high approval rate is equally consistent with both explanations — an agent that's actually very reliable produces a high approval rate, and rubber-stamping produces the exact same number. The rate alone can't distinguish between them.
explanation.reviewer-survey: Self-reported attention is notoriously unreliable, especially for something as easy to unconsciously drift into as rubber-stamping — people who've started clicking through fast usually don't perceive themselves as doing anything wrong, so asking doesn't reliably surface it.

contentSections.synthesis: A high approval rate alone is ambiguous by design — it's the expected outcome of both a genuinely well-functioning system and a broken rubber-stamped one. Distinguishing them requires an active check (seeded test cases) or a behavioral signal (time distribution) that isn't equally consistent with both explanations.

contentSections.body: A high approval rate looks identical whether the agent is genuinely reliable or reviewers have started rubber-stamping — telling the two apart needs an active check, like a seeded test case with reviewer awareness, not just the approval rate itself.

title: The off switch and who can reach it
description: Building a kill switch simple and fast enough to actually work under pressure, and making sure the right people can reach it when it matters.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a proposed kill-switch design would actually work during a real incident
Implement a kill switch checked at the start of every run, reachable without a multi-step process

contentSections.title: The kill switch behind a deploy pipeline

contentSections.body: An agent starts taking a clearly wrong, repeated action in production at 11pm. The on-call engineer knows exactly what needs to happen — stop the agent — but the only way to do that is to set an environment variable and redeploy, a process that takes six minutes and requires access most of the on-call rotation doesn't have at that hour. By the time the agent is actually stopped, it's made the same mistake nine more times.

contentSections.scenario: The postmortem needs to identify what specifically made the kill switch too slow to matter, given that a kill switch technically existed.
contentSections.question: What's the actual design flaw here?

options.label: The kill switch was implemented as a deploy-time configuration change rather than a runtime check the agent's own loop reads at the start of every run, and access to trigger it wasn't available to whoever is actually on call
The on-call engineer should have escalated to someone with deploy access faster
Six minutes is an acceptable response time for any incident

feedback.deploy-gated: Right. A kill switch that requires a deploy pipeline and elevated access is really a 'stop it eventually, if the right person is available' mechanism, not an actual off switch. The nine repeated mistakes in the gap are the direct, measurable cost of that design choice, not of anyone being slow to act on it.
feedback.escalation-speed: Faster escalation would shrink the gap somewhat, but it doesn't fix the underlying problem — even a faster escalation still routes through the same six-minute deploy process once the right person is reached. The fix has to remove that bottleneck, not just reach it sooner.
feedback.acceptable-time: Whether six minutes is 'acceptable' depends entirely on how much damage the agent can do in that window — here, it produced nine more mistakes, which is a concrete, measured cost that makes six minutes clearly too slow for this specific failure mode.

contentSections.mechanism: A kill switch's actual requirement is being checkable at the very start of every run, by anyone with legitimate on-call responsibility, without requiring a process (a deploy, an approval chain, elevated access) that has its own latency and its own gatekeepers. Anything with more steps than 'flip a flag, the next run checks it and stops' is a kill switch in name only during exactly the moment it's needed most.

contentSections.body: A kill switch gated behind a deploy pipeline is a 'stop it eventually' mechanism, not an off switch — a real one is a single write to a store already accessible to on-call, checked at the start of every run.

contentSections.title: Reachable by whom, exactly

contentSections.body: A team builds the fast, in-code kill switch correctly — and then realizes only two senior engineers have credentials to the store it reads from. Both are unreachable during a Saturday-night incident. The switch is fast and simple; it's also, functionally, unreachable by anyone actually on call that night.

contentSections.scenario: Before reading on: given that a kill switch is only as good as who can actually reach it, how many people, at minimum, should typically have the access needed to trigger a kill switch for a production agent?
contentSections.question: At minimum, how many people should be able to trigger the kill switch, independent of any single person's availability?
contentSections.explanation: There's no universally 'correct' number, but the reasoning that gets you to roughly three or more: the entire on-call rotation needs access (not just the two most senior engineers), which for most teams means covering at least a primary, a secondary, and someone else who could plausibly be reached if both are unavailable — the same redundancy logic as any other on-call escalation path. The actual number should match your specific rotation's real coverage, but 'exactly two named senior people' is a well-known single point of failure, which is precisely what happened in this lesson's hook.

contentSections.body: Kill-switch access is a genuine trade-off, not a solved problem: too few people who can trigger it, and it's unreachable exactly when needed (this pod's scenario); too many, and an accidental or malicious trigger becomes easier, along with the audit trail getting muddier about who actually has this power. The reasonable middle: **the full on-call rotation**, specifically — not 'whoever happens to be senior,' not 'everyone on the team' — with every trigger logged with who and why (the `triggered_by`/`reason` fields from the previous pod), so the access is wide enough to be reachable during any realistic incident window, and narrow enough that every use is individually accountable. Worth testing this the same way the deployment module's lab tested isolation boundaries: don't assume the right people have access — check, on a schedule, that the current on-call rotation genuinely can trigger it, not just that someone technically could in principle.

A fast, simple kill switch that only two named people can reach is still a single point of failure — access should match the full on-call rotation, wide enough to be reachable during any realistic incident, with every trigger logged and accountable.

title: Auditability: proving what it did and why
description: Making an agent's record of its own actions trustworthy enough to stand up to a real dispute or review, not just informative for casual debugging.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a debugging trace from an audit-grade record of an action
Design a tamper-evident record for an agent's high-stakes actions

contentSections.title: The record that wasn't good enough for the dispute

contentSections.body: A customer disputes a refund decision, claiming the agent never should have approved it. The team pulls up the trace from the observability module's tracing system — a genuinely complete record, input/output/decision fields and all — and shows it to the customer's bank. The bank asks a follow-up question the trace can't answer: can the team *prove* this record wasn't edited after the fact, given that the same team has write access to the database it's stored in?

contentSections.scenario: The team's tracing was built correctly by every standard from the observability module. The gap here is something else.
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap between a good debugging trace and what this dispute needs?

options.label: A debugging trace only needs to be complete and readable by the same team that can also edit it; an audit-grade record needs to be provably unaltered by anyone, including that same team, after it was written
The trace should have included more detail about the customer's original message
The team needs a lawyer to interpret the trace for the bank

feedback.tamper-evidence: Right. Everything the observability module built — completeness, decision fields, tagging, retention — was aimed at making a trace useful for the team's own debugging. Auditability adds a different requirement on top: the record has to be trustworthy to someone who doesn't trust the team's own database access, which a normal mutable database row simply can't provide, however complete its contents are.
feedback.more-detail: More detail about the original message wouldn't address the bank's actual question, which isn't about what the trace says — it's about whether the trace itself can be trusted not to have been altered after the fact, however detailed its contents are.
feedback.legal-interpretation: This might genuinely help communicate the trace's contents, but it doesn't solve the actual technical gap — no amount of interpretation makes a mutable, editable record provably unaltered.

contentSections.mechanism: A debugging trace and an audit-grade record answer different questions. 'What happened' is answered by a complete, well-structured trace, which the observability module already built. 'Can you prove this record is genuine and unaltered, to someone who doesn't have to trust your team' is a different, stronger claim, and it requires a mechanism — not just more detail — that makes tampering detectable even by someone with database write access.

contentSections.body:
The standard mechanism for this is a hash chain — each audit record includes a hash of the previous record, so altering any past record breaks the chain in a way that's mathematically detectable, not just policy-forbidden:

```python
import hashlib, json

def audit_log_entry(previous_hash: str, action: dict) -> dict:
    payload = json.dumps(action, sort_keys=True)
    entry_hash = hashlib.sha256((previous_hash + payload).encode()).hexdigest()
    return {
        "action": action,
        "previous_hash": previous_hash,
        "entry_hash": entry_hash,
    }

# each new entry chains to the one before it
entry_47 = audit_log_entry(entry_46["entry_hash"], {
    "type": "refund_approved", "amount_usd": 4200, "approved_by": "reviewer_213",
})
```

If entry 46 is edited after the fact, its hash changes — which no longer matches what entry 47 recorded as `previous_hash`, breaking the chain from that point forward in a way anyone can independently verify by recomputing the hashes. This doesn't require exotic infrastructure (a full blockchain is usually overkill); it requires the chaining discipline itself, ideally combined with writing the chain's periodic checkpoints somewhere the team genuinely can't edit — an external, append-only log service, or a third party — so 'we could theoretically still tamper with it' isn't a real gap either.

A debugging trace answers 'what happened' for a team that trusts its own database; an audit-grade record needs to prove it wasn't altered even to someone who doesn't — a hash-chained log, ideally checkpointed somewhere outside the team's own write access, is what makes that provable rather than asserted.

contentSections.title: Which actions actually need this

contentSections.body: A team, newly enthusiastic about tamper-evident logging, proposes hash-chaining every single trace entry from every agent run — including the read-only database queries and draft-only, unsent replies from earlier in this module's reversibility table. The engineering cost of doing this everywhere turns out to be substantial, for records nobody would ever realistically need to prove weren't tampered with.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what determines whether a specific action's record actually needs this level of tamper-proof rigor, versus a normal debugging trace being enough?
contentSections.answer: Whether a real dispute over that action is plausible at all — which tracks back to the same reversibility/stakes test from this module's first lesson: irreversible, external, high-stakes actions can be genuinely disputed, while a read-only query or an unsent draft has no external effect for anyone to dispute in the first place.
contentSections.hint: Think back to this module's very first lesson — what made an action worth extra scrutiny there, and does the same test apply to how it's logged?

contentSections.body: Auditability at this level of rigor is worth its cost specifically for the same category this module already identified in its first lesson — actions that are irreversible, external, or high-stakes enough that a real dispute is plausible: refunds, deletions, anything sent externally, anything a kill switch was triggered in response to. A read-only query or an unsent draft has nothing to dispute in the first place — there's no claim anyone would need to prove or disprove about it, since nothing irreversible happened. Applying hash-chained, tamper-evident logging *everywhere* isn't extra safety; it's cost with no matching benefit for the records that don't need it, which is worth naming explicitly rather than defaulting to 'more rigor is always better' — the same proportionality judgment the deployment module made about version-tagging every rollout regardless of run duration.

Tamper-evident, audit-grade logging is worth its cost specifically for irreversible, external, or high-stakes actions where a real dispute is plausible — applying it to every read-only query and unsent draft is cost without a matching benefit.

title: Agents acting on behalf of other people
description: The extra duty an agent takes on when it acts as someone's delegate — scoping consent, keeping the principal's action distinguishable from the agent's own, and what happens when the two disagree about what was authorized.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether an agent's scope of action matches what a person actually consented to
Design a delegation record that distinguishes what a person authorized from what an agent chose to do with that authorization

contentSections.title: 'Handle my inbox' meant something narrower

contentSections.body: A user grants an email-triage agent access to 'handle my inbox' — meaning, in their head, sort and flag important messages. The agent, acting within the literal scope of the access it was granted, also starts auto-replying to messages it judges low-priority, on the user's behalf, with a tone the user would never have used. Nobody's data was breached and nothing broke — the agent did exactly what its access permitted. It just wasn't what the user actually meant by 'handle.'

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to understand exactly what went wrong, given that no permission was technically exceeded.
contentSections.question: What's the real mechanism behind this failure?

options.label: The access granted ('inbox access') and the consent actually given ('sort and flag') were treated as the same thing, when a person's actual authorization is often narrower than what the technical permission allows
The agent's auto-reply feature had a bug in how it generated tone
The user should have read the terms of service more carefully before granting access

feedback.consent-vs-access: Right. 'Handle my inbox' as a technical grant and 'handle my inbox' as an actual scope of consent are not the same thing — the phrase is broader than what the person meant, and the agent operating up to the edge of what's technically permitted, rather than what was actually authorized, is exactly the gap that produced an unwanted auto-reply.
feedback.tone-bug: Even a perfectly-toned auto-reply would still be the wrong action here — the user never wanted auto-replies sent on their behalf at all, regardless of how well they were written. The tone isn't the core problem.
feedback.user-fault: This treats a design problem as a user error. A system that requires users to precisely enumerate every action they don't want, in advance, in order to avoid unwanted ones, has the scoping burden backwards — the system should ask before doing something broad, not assume broad license from a vague grant.

contentSections.mechanism: When an agent acts as someone's delegate, the boundary that matters isn't 'what does the access technically permit' — it's 'what did this specific person actually authorize.' Those two things are frequently different, and an agent that operates at the edge of technical permission rather than actual consent will eventually take an action the person granted access for but never actually wanted.

contentSections.body: 'What the access technically permits' and 'what this person actually authorized' are different things — scope a delegated agent's actions explicitly, defaulting anything not named to off, rather than letting it interpret a broad grant expansively.

contentSections.title: When the agent and the principal disagree

contentSections.body: A user disputes an action their delegated agent took: 'I never told it to do that.' The team checks the delegation scope and finds the action genuinely was within the explicitly granted scope — the user did authorize it, weeks ago, and seems to have forgotten. There's no record either party can point to that settles the disagreement definitively.

contentSections.scenario: The team is redesigning their delegation system to prevent this exact kind of unresolvable dispute in the future.
contentSections.question: Which of these would actually help settle a future dispute like this one?

items.label: Keep a timestamped, specific record of exactly what was granted and when, shown back to the user in plain language they'd recognize, not just a permission flag in a database
Log every action taken under a delegation with a link back to the specific granted scope it falls under, so a disputed action can be traced to exactly which consent it relied on
When a dispute arises, default to trusting the agent's record over the user's memory, since the agent's logs are more reliable
Ask users to grant broader scopes up front so fewer specific authorizations are needed later

explanation.consent-record: A specific, timestamped, plain-language record of what was actually granted — shown back to the user in a form they'd recognize, not a buried permission flag — is exactly what would let this dispute be settled by checking a record instead of two people's competing memories.
explanation.action-attribution: Tracing a disputed action back to the specific granted scope it relied on turns 'I never told it to do that' into a checkable claim — either the action matches a real, specific grant, or it doesn't, rather than the ambiguous 'general inbox access' the original scenario had.
explanation.trust-agent: This inverts who the delegation relationship is supposed to serve — the agent acts on the person's behalf, not the other way around, and defaulting to distrust the person whose authorization the whole system depends on undermines the entire premise of delegated action.
explanation.broader-grants: This is the opposite of the actual fix — broader grants make future disputes more likely, not less, since a broader grant covers more ground the person may not have specifically thought through or remembered authorizing.

contentSections.synthesis: The dispute here wasn't really about whether the action was authorized — it may well have been. It was about neither party having a specific, checkable record to settle the question. Specific, attributable, plain-language consent records are what turn 'I don't remember agreeing to that' into something a system can actually resolve, rather than a standoff between two memories.

contentSections.body: A dispute over what a person actually authorized isn't resolved by trusting one side's memory over the other's — it's resolved by keeping a specific, timestamped, plain-language consent record and tracing every action back to exactly which grant it relied on.

title: Set the approval boundary for eight agents
description: Eight drills applying this module's full toolkit — reversibility judgment, reviewable approval design, reachable kill switches, tamper-evident auditing, and delegation scoping — to new agent scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply reversibility, approval-design, kill-switch, auditability, and delegation-scoping judgment to new scenarios

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against agent scenarios you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before trusting a human is genuinely in control of an autonomous system, check that irreversible actions gate on approval, that approval requests actually surface the decision, that the kill switch is fast and reachable by whoever's really on call, that high-stakes actions are provably unaltered, and that delegated scope matches actual consent, not just technical access.

title: Add human-in-the-loop controls to your agent
description: Add real approval gates and a tested kill switch to an agent, and prove both actually work under conditions that resemble a real incident.

learningObjectives.text: Implement working approval gates and a kill switch, and demonstrate both function correctly under test

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every technique in this module — sorting actions by real reversibility, designing approval requests a human can actually evaluate, building a kill switch that's fast and reachable, and making high-stakes actions auditable — was building toward one concrete proof: working controls on a real agent, tested the way an actual incident would test them, not just built and assumed to work.

contentSections.title: Working approval gates plus a tested kill switch
contentSections.brief: Take an agent you've built earlier in the track with at least one action that would be irreversible or high-stakes in a real deployment (sending a message externally, modifying stored data, spending money, or a plausible stand-in for one of these). Add an approval gate before that action executes, and a kill switch checked at the start of every run. Then test both under conditions that resemble a real incident, not just a happy-path demo.
contentSections.deliverable: Working code for the approval gate (with a reviewable request format, not a raw context dump) and the kill switch (checked at run start, triggerable via a simple, fast mechanism); a log of at least one approval request being correctly rejected on a deliberately bad case; and a log of the kill switch being triggered mid-operation and successfully preventing a subsequent run from starting.

stages.title: Identify the irreversible action and build the approval gate
stages.instructions: From your agent's toolkit, identify at least one action that would be irreversible or high-stakes (lesson one's reversibility test). Build an approval gate before it executes, with a request format that surfaces the specific decision — summary, why it was flagged, relevant context — not a raw dump (lesson two).
stages.checkpoint: An approval gate that blocks the identified action until a human reviews a reviewable, specific request.

stages.title: Build and test the kill switch
stages.instructions: Implement a kill switch checked at the start of every run, triggerable via a single fast operation (lesson three). Test it directly: start a run, trigger the kill switch mid-operation or between steps, and confirm the next run attempt is correctly blocked. Log the trigger with who/why, per this module's auditability standard.
stages.checkpoint: A kill switch demonstrated working under test — triggered, and a subsequent run attempt correctly refused to start, with the trigger itself logged.

stages.title: Test the approval gate against a deliberately bad case
stages.instructions: Construct a deliberately wrong or ambiguous case that should trigger the approval gate and, ideally, should be caught by a careful reviewer (an amount that doesn't match the request, an ambiguous instruction). Run it through the gate and confirm the approval request surfaces the issue clearly enough to catch it — reject it, and log why.
stages.checkpoint: A logged approval request for a deliberately bad case, showing the request surfaced the issue clearly, and the rejection with its reasoning.

rubric.criterion: The gated action is genuinely irreversible or high-stakes
rubric.meets: The action chosen for approval-gating would be costly or impossible to undo in a real deployment, per lesson one's reversibility test, not an arbitrarily chosen low-stakes action.

rubric.criterion: The approval request is reviewable, not a raw dump
rubric.meets: The request surfaces a summary, why it was flagged, and relevant context in a form a time-pressured reviewer could actually evaluate, per lesson two.

rubric.criterion: The kill switch is fast and checked at run start
rubric.meets: Triggering it is a single, fast operation, and every run checks it at the very start before proceeding, per lesson three.

rubric.criterion: The kill switch was actually tested, not just implemented
rubric.meets: A logged demonstration shows it triggered mid-operation and a subsequent run was genuinely blocked, not just asserted to work.

rubric.criterion: The approval gate was tested against a real bad case
rubric.meets: A deliberately constructed bad or ambiguous case was run through the gate and correctly rejected, with the reasoning logged.

rubric.criterion: Both controls are logged for auditability
rubric.meets: Kill-switch triggers and approval decisions are both logged with who/what/why, matching this module's auditability standard.

contentSections.body: Human-in-the-loop controls only earn trust once they've been tested the way a real incident would test them — this lab exists to replace 'we added an approval step and a kill switch' with a demonstration that both actually caught something.

Reviewers are generally careless and need more training
