title: Drift: it stopped working and nothing changed
description: Why an agent's quality can degrade over months with no code change on your side, and how to catch that it's happening before someone else reports it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how an agent's real-world environment can change underneath a codebase that never changed
Identify likely sources of drift for a given agent's specific dependencies

contentSections.title: Nobody touched the code

contentSections.body: A pricing-lookup agent that scrapes a competitor's website has worked reliably for four months. In month five, its accuracy quietly drops to near zero. The team checks their git history — no commits in the last six weeks. Nobody deployed anything. Nobody changed a prompt, a tool, or a line of code. The agent simply stopped working, for reasons that have nothing to do with anything the team did.

contentSections.scenario: The team needs to figure out what could possibly cause a failure with zero code changes on their end.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation, given that nothing on the team's side changed?

options.label: Something the agent depends on but doesn't control — the competitor's website structure, in this case — changed independently, and the agent's tool logic, built for the old structure, silently stopped matching the new one
The model itself has been quietly getting worse over time at a fixed task
This can't actually happen — something on the team's side must have changed even if git history shows nothing

feedback.external-drift: Right. An agent's correctness depends not just on its own code, prompt, and model, but on the state of everything it reads from or acts on — and none of those are under the team's control or version-tracked in their own repository. A website's HTML structure, an API's response schema, a data source's format — any of these can change independently, silently breaking an agent that was built assuming they'd stay the same.
feedback.model-decay: Models don't degrade at a fixed task simply from the passage of time with no changes — if the exact same model version is still being called the same way, its behavior on a fixed input is stable. Something external is a far more likely explanation than the model itself spontaneously worsening.
feedback.impossible: This is exactly the intuition drift exists to correct — 'nothing changed' from the team's own commit history is genuinely consistent with something real changing, just somewhere the team doesn't control or track.

contentSections.mechanism: 'It worked before and nothing changed' quietly assumes 'nothing changed' means the whole system, when it really only means the team's own codebase. An agent's actual environment includes every external thing it depends on — websites it scrapes, APIs it calls, data formats it parses — and none of those show up in a git diff when they change. Drift is what happens when that gap between 'my code is stable' and 'my environment is stable' becomes visible as a failure.

contentSections.body:
A short taxonomy of where drift typically comes from, useful for narrowing down an investigation instead of starting from zero:

- **Structural drift** — a website's HTML changes, an API's response schema adds/removes/renames a field, breaking parsing logic built for the old shape.
- **Distributional drift** — the *kind* of input the agent sees shifts over time (customer questions trend toward a new topic, documents start arriving in a new format) even though nothing about the agent's own tools broke.
- **Behavioral drift on the far side** — something the agent depends on changes its actual behavior, not just its shape: a competitor changes pricing strategy in a way that makes old assumptions about 'typical' prices wrong, a third-party service starts rate-limiting more aggressively.

The pricing-lookup agent's failure is structural drift — the site's HTML almost certainly changed. Knowing which category a suspected drift falls into narrows the investigation considerably: structural drift means diffing the actual current source against what the parsing logic expects; distributional drift means comparing recent inputs against the original eval set's distribution; far-side behavioral drift means checking whether the *meaning* of a still-correctly-parsed value has changed.

'Nothing changed' usually means 'nothing in my own codebase changed' — an agent's real environment includes every external thing it depends on, and any of those can drift independently, silently, with zero signal in your own commit history.

contentSections.title: Catching it before the complaint does

contentSections.body: The pricing agent's near-zero accuracy was discovered because a customer complained about a wildly wrong price — five weeks after the drift actually started. Nothing in the team's monitoring caught it earlier, because their only quality signal was 'did the tool call succeed without throwing an error,' and a scraper that successfully returns the wrong data because the page structure changed doesn't throw any error at all.

contentSections.scenario: The team is redesigning their monitoring to catch structural drift like this within days, not five weeks.
contentSections.question: Which of these would actually help catch this kind of silent drift earlier?

items.label: Periodically re-run a small, fixed eval set with known-correct answers against the live agent, and alert if accuracy drops meaningfully from baseline
Add a lightweight sanity check on the scraped data's shape (does the price look like a plausible number in a plausible range, not garbage or empty)
Keep relying solely on the tool-call error/success rate, since that's already being tracked
Continue treating customer complaints as the primary detection mechanism, since they're already a reliable signal

explanation.eval-rerun: This directly catches drift of any kind, structural or otherwise — a fixed eval set with known-correct answers, re-run periodically against the live system, will show accuracy dropping the moment the underlying data source stops matching what the parsing logic expects, regardless of whether any individual call 'errors.'
explanation.shape-check: A cheap sanity check on the output's plausibility (is this a real-looking price, not null or garbage) catches a specific, common symptom of structural drift — a scraper returning nonsense because the selector it's using no longer matches anything meaningful on the changed page.
explanation.error-rate-only: This is exactly what already failed here — the scraper succeeded, in the narrow sense of not throwing an exception, while returning wrong data. An error rate that stays flat during a real quality collapse is providing false reassurance, not real monitoring.
explanation.wait-for-complaints: Relying on complaints as the detection mechanism means the failure runs, unnoticed, for however long it takes someone to notice and report it — five weeks in this case. This is detection by accident, not a design choice.

contentSections.synthesis: The gap here wasn't a lack of monitoring — it was monitoring the wrong signal. 'Did the call succeed without erroring' and 'is the data actually correct' are different questions, and structural drift specifically produces failures that pass the first test while failing the second. Catching it early means checking correctness periodically, not just success.

contentSections.body: A tool call succeeding without an error and a tool call returning correct data are different claims — structural drift specifically breaks the second while leaving the first intact, so catching drift early means periodically checking correctness against known answers, not just watching the error rate.

title: Model deprecations and migration
description: Migrating to a new model version deliberately, with real testing, instead of being forced into it by a deprecation deadline with no evidence the new version behaves the same.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a model version deprecation forces a real migration decision, not a drop-in swap
Design a migration process that verifies quality before cutting over fully

contentSections.title: The deprecation email nobody planned for

contentSections.body: A model provider announces that a specific model version will stop being served in 90 days. A team's agent pins that exact version in its config. With three weeks left before the deadline, they finally swap in the newer version — no testing beyond 'does it still respond' — and ship it, because the deadline is close and there's no time left to do anything more thorough.

The core mistake here isn't the swap itself — a model provider deprecating an old version is a completely normal, expected part of operating anything long-term, not a crisis. The mistake is treating the swap as something that can happen the same week a hard deadline forces it, with no room for the actual work: a new model version, even a nominally 'better' successor, is not guaranteed to behave identically on your specific prompts and tasks. It can be more literal, less literal, handle edge cases differently, or simply produce a different distribution of outputs on the exact eval set that validated the old version — none of which shows up by just confirming it responds.

The fix is treating a deprecation announcement as the start of a migration process with a real timeline, not the final week before the deadline:

```python
MIGRATION_TIMELINE = {
    'deprecation_announced': 'day 0',
    'run_eval_set_against_new_version': 'day 3-7',
    'compare_results_to_baseline': 'day 7-10',
    'fix_regressions_found': 'day 10-30',       # this is where real time is usually needed
    'canary_rollout_to_new_version': 'day 30-45',
    'full_cutover_before_deadline': 'day 45-90', # real margin before the hard deadline
}
```

The critical resource here is time for step four — fixing whatever regressions the eval set actually reveals — which is exactly the step a three-week, deadline-driven scramble has no room for.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to name precisely what's risky about their three-week, no-testing swap, beyond 'it feels rushed.'
contentSections.question: What's the specific risk this approach doesn't address?

options.label: There's no evidence the new model version performs comparably on this agent's actual tasks — 'it responds' says nothing about whether it responds correctly on the cases that matter
Newer model versions are always strictly worse than older ones at every task
Model providers should never deprecate old versions

feedback.no-evidence: Right. The specific gap is evidence, not intuition about direction — a newer model might genuinely be better on average and still regress on specific cases this agent's particular prompts and tasks depend on. 'It responds' checks that the API contract still basically works; it says nothing about whether the actual task still gets done correctly.
feedback.always-worse: This isn't generally true — provider upgrades are frequently genuine improvements. The point isn't that newer is worse, it's that 'probably better on average' isn't the same claim as 'verified to still work correctly on this agent's specific tasks.'
feedback.no-deprecation: Deprecations are a completely normal, expected part of using any managed model API long-term — the problem in this scenario isn't that a deprecation happened, it's that the team had no process ready for when it inevitably would.

contentSections.mechanism: A model swap is a change to the single most important component of an agent's behavior, and this track's whole evaluation phase exists because 'it seems to work' isn't evidence for a system like this. Skipping evaluation on a swap because a deadline is close doesn't remove the need for evidence — it just removes the evidence, while the risk stays exactly the same.

contentSections.body: A model version deprecation is a normal, expected event — the risk isn't the deprecation, it's swapping in a new version with no evidence it performs comparably on your specific tasks, which a deadline-driven, testing-skipped scramble guarantees you won't have.

contentSections.title: What the eval set actually needs to catch here

contentSections.body: A team does run their eval set against the new model version before cutting over — and it passes at 91%, comparable to the old version's 93% baseline. They ship it. Two weeks later, a specific category of task — one slightly underrepresented in the eval set — turns out to have regressed badly, hidden inside the overall aggregate number.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: how can an eval score drop only 2 points overall while one specific category has actually collapsed?
contentSections.answer: If the collapsed category is a small enough slice of the total eval set, a severe drop within it barely moves the overall weighted average — the aggregate number is a blend, and a bad result in a small slice gets diluted almost completely by good results everywhere else.
contentSections.hint: Think about what an average actually does to a large change in a small subgroup versus a large group.

contentSections.body:
An aggregate pass rate can hide a real regression the same way a single 'average latency' number can hide a slow tail — this is the same lesson from the evaluation phase of this track about stratifying results, applied specifically to a migration decision. A migration check needs to compare per-category performance, not just the overall number:

| Task category | Old version | New version | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Simple lookup | 96% | 97% | +1% |
| Multi-step reasoning | 94% | 95% | +1% |
| Edge-case formatting | 89% | 61% | **-28%** |

The overall aggregate (93% → 91%) looks like a small, acceptable dip. The category breakdown shows a real, specific regression the aggregate almost completely absorbed, because edge-case formatting was a small enough slice of the eval set that its collapse barely moved the overall number. A migration decision needs the category-level view specifically because 'the average is fine' and 'nothing regressed' are different claims, and only the aggregate one is what a quick pass/fail check would show.

An aggregate eval score comparable to baseline can hide a real regression in an underrepresented category — a migration decision needs the per-category breakdown, not just the overall number, or a genuine collapse in one area can ship unnoticed.

title: Tool and API changes underneath you
description: Surviving a breaking change in an upstream tool or API your agent depends on — detecting it fast, and building contract checks that catch it before a real run does.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a breaking upstream API change from a transient failure
Design a contract test that catches an upstream schema change before it reaches a production run

contentSections.title: The field that quietly became optional

contentSections.body: An agent calls a third-party shipping-rates API as one of its tools. The API provider ships a version update — announced in a changelog nobody on the team reads regularly — that makes a previously-always-present `estimated_days` field optional, present only for certain carriers. The agent's code, written assuming the field always exists, starts throwing an unhandled exception on every call to a carrier that no longer includes it, mid-run, with no graceful handling.

contentSections.scenario: The team's on-call engineer is trying to figure out whether this is a bug in their own agent's logic or something that changed upstream.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that turned a routine API update into a production incident?

options.label: The agent's code had an implicit assumption (this field always exists) that was never checked, so when the upstream contract changed, the failure showed up as an unhandled exception deep in the agent's own logic rather than a clear, early signal that the contract itself had changed
The shipping API provider made an unreasonable, unannounced breaking change
The agent should never depend on third-party APIs for critical functionality

feedback.implicit-assumption: Right. The API change itself was announced (in a changelog, even if nobody was reading it) and, from a strict versioning standpoint, a field becoming optional rather than being removed outright is often considered backward-compatible by the provider. The actual failure is downstream: the agent's own code never made its assumption about that field explicit or checked it, so the change surfaced as a confusing runtime crash instead of a clear, contained, early signal.
feedback.unreasonable-provider: A field going from always-present to conditionally-present is a fairly common and often-considered-compatible kind of change from an API provider's perspective — the problem isn't that the provider did something unreasonable, it's that the consuming code had no defense against a change like this actually happening.
feedback.no-third-party: Avoiding all third-party dependencies isn't a realistic or even generally good response — most useful agents need real external tools and APIs. The fix has to be resilience to upstream change, not avoidance of all upstream dependencies.

contentSections.mechanism: Any code that consumes an external API is making an implicit contract with it — this response will always have this shape. That contract is never actually guaranteed by the provider to stay frozen forever, and when it changes, code that never made its assumptions explicit fails in whatever way happens to be closest to the point of use, which is often a confusing, unhelpful crash rather than a clear signal that 'the contract changed.'

contentSections.body: Any code consuming an external API is making an implicit contract with it about the response's shape — making that assumption explicit and checked turns an upstream change from a confusing crash into a clear, handled, debuggable signal.

contentSections.title: Catching it before a real run does

contentSections.body: The explicit check helps once the change has already happened and been noticed in production — but the team wants to know about a breaking upstream change *before* a real customer-facing run hits it, the same way they'd want to know about a code regression before it ships.

contentSections.code:
# "testing" the shipping API integration
def test_shipping_api():
    response = call_shipping_api(test_package)
    assert response is not None  # passes even if the response shape changed completely
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this test, given the team's actual goal of catching a breaking upstream change early?

options.label: The assertion only checks that a response came back at all — it doesn't check the response's actual shape, so a contract change that alters or removes fields (exactly what caused the incident) would pass this test with no warning
The test should call the real API less often to save cost
The test package used isn't realistic enough

feedback.no-shape-check: Right. 'Is not None' would have passed throughout the entire incident described in this lesson — the response was never None, it just had a different shape than the code assumed. A test built to catch exactly this failure needs to check the specific fields and their presence, not just that a response arrived.
feedback.call-frequency: Call frequency is a reasonable cost consideration for a scheduled contract test, but it's unrelated to why this specific test would have missed the incident — the problem is what the test checks, not how often it runs.
feedback.test-data: The realism of the test package isn't the core issue here — even a perfectly realistic package would trigger a response that this shallow assertion would still pass, since it only checks for a non-null response.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A real contract test checks the response's actual structure against an explicit schema, run on a schedule independent of any real customer traffic: `assert 'estimated_days' in response, "contract check failed: estimated_days missing from shipping API response"` for each field the agent's code actually depends on. Run daily (or more often for critical dependencies), this catches a breaking change within hours of it happening, rather than waiting for it to surface as a production incident during a real run.

contentSections.body: A scheduled contract test — hitting the real upstream API on a schedule and checking the response against the exact shape the agent's code depends on — is the migration-testing discipline from the previous lesson applied continuously, rather than only at the moment of a deliberate model swap. The two failure modes it guards against are the same ones this module has been building toward all along: silent drift (the API changed and nobody noticed until a customer did) and a confusing production crash (the change surfaced as an unhandled exception instead of a clear signal). A contract test that runs independently of real traffic, checking the specific fields the code actually relies on, catches the change on its own schedule instead of on whatever schedule real customer traffic happens to hit it.

A test that only checks 'did a response come back' will pass straight through a breaking contract change — a real contract test checks the response's actual shape against what the code depends on, run on its own schedule, so a breaking upstream change is caught in hours instead of during a real production run.

title: A maintenance routine that fits a bad month
description: Designing a recurring maintenance routine light enough to actually survive a busy or difficult stretch, instead of one that only works when someone has a spare week to spend on it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate why an ambitious maintenance plan tends to fail during exactly the periods it's most needed
Design a minimal, sustainable maintenance routine that degrades gracefully under time pressure

contentSections.title: The maintenance plan that only survived good months

contentSections.body: A team writes an ambitious maintenance plan: full eval-set re-run weekly, dependency audit monthly, a detailed changelog review of every upstream API and model provider. It works well for the first six weeks. Then a busy quarter hits — the same person responsible for maintenance is pulled onto three other things — and the plan quietly stops happening entirely, not scaled back, just abandoned, because there was never a version of it that fit into a bad week.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to understand why the plan failed completely instead of just slipping a little during the busy quarter.
contentSections.question: What's the actual design flaw in how the maintenance plan was built?

options.label: The plan had only one mode — the full version — with nothing lighter to fall back to, so when full capacity wasn't available, the only options were 'do all of it' or 'do none of it,' and 'none of it' is what a genuinely busy period produces
Weekly eval reruns are inherently too frequent for any team to sustain
The person responsible for maintenance simply wasn't reliable enough

feedback.no-graceful-degradation: Right. A plan with only a full, ambitious mode and no lighter fallback isn't actually a plan for a bad month — it's a plan for every month being a good month. Once that stopped being true, there was no smaller version to fall back to, so the whole thing lapsed rather than degrading gracefully to something smaller but still real.
feedback.too-frequent: Frequency alone isn't the core issue — a weekly cadence can work fine for a team with the capacity, and the same team might sustain even more frequent light checks if they were cheap enough. The problem is the plan had no lighter version at all, not that its single version was too demanding.
feedback.person-fault: This treats a structural gap as an individual failing — the same thing would likely have happened to almost anyone given three competing priorities and a maintenance plan with no smaller fallback mode built in. The fix is in the plan's design, not the person.

contentSections.mechanism: This is the same energy-aware design principle this track's own curriculum architecture is built on, applied to an operations routine instead of a lesson plan: a plan that assumes consistent full capacity will work exactly as long as capacity stays consistently full, and collapse entirely the first time it doesn't — the fix is a plan with an explicit lighter mode, not a plan that assumes the good conditions it was designed under will hold indefinitely.

contentSections.body:
A maintenance routine that survives a bad month needs at least two tiers, with the lighter one cheap enough that skipping it is never the path of least resistance:

```python
MAINTENANCE_ROUTINE = {
    'always': {  # ~10 minutes, cannot reasonably be skipped even in a bad week
        'check_kill_switch_reachable': 'weekly',
        'check_spend_within_budget': 'weekly',
        'skim_error_rate_dashboard': 'weekly',
    },
    'full': {  # the ambitious version, for weeks with real capacity
        'rerun_full_eval_set': 'weekly',
        'review_all_upstream_changelogs': 'monthly',
        'audit_all_dependencies_for_deprecation_notices': 'monthly',
    },
}
```

The 'always' tier is deliberately small — a handful of minutes, covering the things whose silent failure would be most costly (an unreachable kill switch, a blown budget) — precisely so it survives a genuinely bad week without competing for the same time as everything else. The 'full' tier catches more, but skipping it in a bad week degrades gracefully to still having the essentials covered, rather than collapsing to nothing at all.

A maintenance plan with only one ambitious mode collapses entirely the first time full capacity isn't available — a sustainable plan has a small, cheap 'always' tier covering the highest-cost failures, so a bad week degrades to something smaller instead of nothing at all.

contentSections.title: Choosing what belongs in the always-tier

contentSections.body: A team building their 'always' tier debates what belongs in it. One person wants to include a full manual review of the last week's flagged conversations — genuinely valuable, but easily 45 minutes if done properly. Another argues that defeats the entire purpose of an 'always' tier.

contentSections.scenario: Before reading on: this module's design goal for an 'always' tier is that it survives a genuinely bad week — one where the person responsible has very little discretionary time.
contentSections.question: Roughly what's a reasonable upper bound, in minutes, for the total weekly time commitment of an 'always' tier that's actually going to survive a bad week?
contentSections.explanation: There's no universal right number, but the reasoning that gets you to something in the 10-15 minute range: it has to be small enough that even someone with almost no discretionary time that week can still plausibly do it, which rules out anything approaching a real task (a 45-minute manual review is a real task, not a quick check). A 45-minute item in the 'always' tier defeats its own purpose — it just recreates the original problem (one mode, too heavy to survive a bad week) one level down, with 'always' as a misleading label on something that isn't actually always going to happen.

contentSections.body: The 45-minute manual review is genuinely valuable — nobody's arguing it isn't — which is exactly why it belongs in the 'full' tier, not the 'always' one. Conflating 'valuable' with 'must happen every single week no matter what' is the same mistake as the original all-or-nothing plan, just with better intentions. The always-tier's job isn't to catch everything worth catching; it's to catch the small number of things whose *silent* failure would be genuinely costly — an unreachable kill switch, a blown budget, an error-rate spike nobody noticed — cheaply enough that doing it is never a real decision. Everything else, however valuable, belongs in a tier that's allowed to slip during a bad month without the whole system quietly stopping.

Something being valuable doesn't automatically qualify it for the 'always' tier — that tier is specifically for the small number of checks whose silent failure would be most costly, kept cheap enough that skipping them is never the easy option, even in a genuinely bad week.

title: Deciding to turn it off
description: Deciding, with real evidence rather than sunk-cost momentum, when an agent should be shut down rather than kept limping along or endlessly re-invested in.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a genuine case for continued investment from sunk-cost momentum keeping a failing agent running
Design sunset criteria for an agent, decided in advance rather than in the moment of the decision

contentSections.title: Eighteen months of patching

contentSections.body: A team has kept a document-classification agent running for eighteen months, patching it after every drift incident, every model deprecation, every upstream schema change this module has covered. Each individual fix was reasonable at the time. Looking at the total engineering hours sunk into keeping it alive over that period, someone finally asks: would we build this again today, given everything we now know about how much upkeep it actually needs? Nobody has a confident answer, because nobody's been tracking the cumulative cost — only reacting to each incident as it came.

contentSections.scenario: The team wants to understand why this question wasn't asked sooner, given eighteen months of visible, individually-reasonable patches.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that let this go unquestioned for so long?

options.label: Each individual patch was evaluated only against 'is this worth fixing right now,' never against the cumulative maintenance cost across all incidents — so no single moment ever triggered the larger question, even though the total answer might be different from any individual one
The team simply lacked the technical skill to build something more maintainable
Eighteen months isn't actually long enough to reasonably ask this question

feedback.no-cumulative-view: Right. 'Is this specific fix worth doing right now' is almost always yes, in isolation — a single afternoon fixing a drift incident is cheap compared to the cost of the agent failing. But that per-incident question never adds up the total, and a system can be individually-reasonable-to-patch at every single incident while being, in aggregate, not worth the ongoing investment compared to alternatives.
feedback.skill-gap: There's no indication of a skill problem here — every individual patch worked. The issue is a missing question at a different level (the cumulative total), not a capability gap at the level where the actual patching happened.
feedback.too-soon: Eighteen months of continuous patching is a substantial, easily long-enough track record to evaluate a real trend against — the issue isn't that the question is premature, it's that nothing prompted anyone to ask it earlier.

contentSections.mechanism: Sunk-cost reasoning doesn't usually show up as an explicit 'we've invested too much to stop now' — it shows up as exactly this: a series of individually reasonable decisions, each evaluated in isolation, that never triggers the larger question because no single decision is where that question belongs. The fix is deciding, in advance, at what point the cumulative pattern itself becomes the thing being evaluated — not waiting for someone to happen to ask.

contentSections.body:
A useful practice: track maintenance incidents as a first-class metric, the same way the cost and observability modules argued for tracking spend and errors as explicit numbers rather than vague impressions:

```python
MAINTENANCE_LOG = [
    {'date': '2025-03-02', 'type': 'drift', 'hours': 6, 'cause': 'source website structure changed'},
    {'date': '2025-05-14', 'type': 'model_deprecation', 'hours': 14, 'cause': 'forced migration, regressions found and fixed'},
    {'date': '2025-08-01', 'type': 'api_breaking_change', 'hours': 4, 'cause': 'shipping API field became optional'},
    # ... eighteen months of entries ...
]

def quarterly_maintenance_review(log):
    total_hours = sum(entry['hours'] for entry in log)
    incident_count = len(log)
    print(f"Last quarter: {incident_count} incidents, {total_hours} engineering hours")
    # the number itself doesn't decide anything — but having it, reviewed on a
    # schedule, is what actually prompts the 'is this still worth it' question
    # instead of leaving it to chance whether anyone happens to add it up
```

The log's real value isn't the individual entries — it's making the *cumulative* cost visible on a recurring schedule, which is what turns 'would we build this again today' from a question nobody happens to ask into a question that gets asked deliberately, on purpose, before eighteen months pass unexamined.

Each individual maintenance fix being worth doing in isolation doesn't mean the cumulative pattern is worth continuing — tracking maintenance cost as an explicit, reviewed number is what turns 'should we still be running this' into a question that gets asked on purpose, instead of one nobody happens to ask.

contentSections.title: Deciding in advance, not in the moment

contentSections.body: Having finally asked the question, the team realizes they have no criteria for answering it — just a gut sense that eighteen months and a growing incident log feels like a lot. Whatever they decide now will be argued about by whoever's emotionally invested in the project having succeeded, which is exactly the kind of decision sunset criteria set in advance are meant to avoid having to make in the heat of the moment.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what specifically goes wrong when sunset criteria get decided in the same meeting as the shutdown decision itself, rather than set in advance?
contentSections.answer: Whoever is most emotionally invested in the system's continued existence has maximum influence over where the bar gets set, because the bar and the decision are being chosen by the same people, at the same time, under the same pressure — deciding the threshold in advance, before anyone knows which way a specific case will fall, removes that conflict of interest.
contentSections.hint: Think about who's in the room for that meeting, and what incentive they have when the threshold itself is still up for grabs.

contentSections.body:
Sunset criteria work the same way the canary rollback threshold and the alert threshold did earlier in this phase: decided in advance, against real numbers, specifically so the decision doesn't have to be made from scratch under the influence of whoever's present and however attached they are to the system's continued existence.

```python
SUNSET_CRITERIA = {
    'maintenance_hours_per_quarter_threshold': 20,   # above this, cost is outpacing value
    'consecutive_quarters_over_threshold': 2,        # one bad quarter isn't a trend
    'alternative_exists': None,  # filled in when evaluated: does a simpler approach now cover this?
    'business_value_still_present': None,  # filled in when evaluated: is this still solving a real problem?
}

def should_evaluate_sunset(maintenance_log, criteria):
    recent_quarters = group_by_quarter(maintenance_log)[-criteria['consecutive_quarters_over_threshold']:]
    all_over = all(q['total_hours'] > criteria['maintenance_hours_per_quarter_threshold'] for q in recent_quarters)
    return all_over  # triggers a deliberate review, not an automatic shutdown
```

Note what this triggers: a deliberate, structured review — not an automatic shutdown. Sunset criteria decide *when to seriously ask the question with real numbers in hand*, not what the answer has to be; a system that's expensive to maintain but still delivering real, otherwise-unavailable value might reasonably survive the review. What the criteria remove is the version of this decision made purely on gut feeling, in a single meeting, by whoever happens to be most emotionally invested in either direction.

Sunset criteria decided in advance don't decide the outcome — they decide when the question gets asked seriously, with real numbers, instead of being settled by gut feeling and whoever in the room is most attached to the system staying alive.

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every technique in this module — diagnosing silent drift, migrating models with real evidence, contract-testing upstream dependencies, designing a maintenance routine that survives a bad month, and setting sunset criteria in advance — was building toward one concrete proof: a runbook specific enough that someone other than you could actually operate this agent for the next year.

contentSections.title: A runbook covering monitoring, common failures, migration and shutdown
contentSections.brief: Write an operations runbook for an agent you've built earlier in the track. It needs to be specific to that agent's actual dependencies and failure modes — not a generic template — and cover what someone unfamiliar with the system would need to keep it running for a year: how to detect drift, what to do when a model or an upstream API changes, what the maintenance routine actually is, and what would trigger seriously considering shutting it down.
contentSections.deliverable: A written runbook with four sections: drift detection (what could drift for this specific agent, and how you'd catch it), migration procedure (how a model or dependency change would be evaluated before cutover, with the specific eval approach), a two-tier maintenance routine (an 'always' tier and a 'full' tier, sized realistically for this agent), and sunset criteria (specific, numeric, decided now rather than left for the moment of crisis).

rubric.criterion: Drift detection is specific to this agent's real dependencies
rubric.meets: Named dependencies (a specific model version, specific APIs or sources) with a real detection method for each, not a generic 'monitor for drift' statement.

rubric.meets: Concrete thresholds (hours, incident counts, time windows) decided now, not a vague statement like 'if it stops being worth it.'
